bill.title: a joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose global tariffs
bill.description: This bill would end the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. A tax on imports is also called a tariff. These taxes are called “reciprocal tariffs.” Ending the emergency would cancel the tariffs based on it: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries. The bill would not end tariffs under other laws.
bill.comparison: If this bill took effect on October 30, 2025, versus law in force then

values.name: Universalism – Nature
statements: to take part in activities to defend nature
to protect the natural environment from destruction or pollution

values.name: Universalism – Concern
statements: that the weak and vulnerable in society be protected
that every person in the world have equal opportunities in life
that everyone be treated justly, even people they don't know

values.name: Universalism – Tolerance
statements: to be tolerant toward all kinds of people and groups
to listen to and understand people who are different to them
to accept people even when they disagree with them

values.name: Security – Personal
statements: to avoid disease and protect their health
to be personally safe and secure
values.reference: Read this value as held by an average American: ordinary personal health and safety risks in U.S. circumstances, without assuming a specially exposed person.

values.name: Security – Societal
statements: that their country is secure and stable
to have a strong state that can defend its citizens
that their country protect itself against all threats
values.reference: Read "their country" as the United States.

values.name: Tradition
statements: to maintain traditional values and ways of thinking
to follow their family's customs or the customs of a religion
to honor the traditional practices of their culture
values.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.

claims.title: The bill ends the April 2 emergency
claims.statement: If enacted, S.J.Res.88 ends the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, in Executive Order 14257, on the date of enactment.
claims.classification_reason: Direct bill text, checked word for word against the packet's bill text. No packet source disputes what the text says.
claims.source_quote: the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution
claims.scope_html: This is the version the Senate approved on October 30, 2025. The comparison is this bill taking effect on that date versus the law in force on that date. The bill names this one emergency only.
claims.background_html: A national emergency is a formal statement by the President that unlocks special legal powers. An executive order is a written order from the President. A joint resolution is a type of bill that becomes law if it is enacted.
claims.support_html: The bill says “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [SES 1]

claims.title: The taxes based on the emergency stop for new imports
claims.statement: When this emergency ends, the extra import taxes imposed because of it stop for new imports at the rates in force that day. Other tariff laws are not ended, and matters already pending or duties already owed are not changed by the ending itself.
claims.classification_reason: Follows directly from the termination law's text applied to taxes the order imposes under this emergency. The packet has no objection; an analysis of ending the same emergency reaches the same result.
claims.source_quote: any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date
claims.scope_html: This covers imports still taxed under this emergency on October 30, 2025. Customs applies these taxes to goods “other than those that fall within the identified exceptions” [SES 3]. For China, covered goods “will be assessed an additional ad valorem duty rate of 10%.” [TR 3] Goods added to the metal tariff lists in August are affected only for their other content: “The non-steel and non-aluminum content will remain subject to the reciprocal and other applicable tariffs.” [UNN 4] The law also says the ending “shall not affect” pending matters or “any rights or duties that matured or penalties that were incurred prior to such date” [SES 2].
claims.background_html: A tariff is a tax on goods brought into a country. The taxes under this emergency are called “reciprocal tariffs”. Later orders changed the rates, but the emergency stayed their basis: “the terms of Executive Order 14257, as amended, shall continue to apply.” [UNN 2]
claims.support_html: Federal law says that when an emergency ends, “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [SES 2]. The Center for American Progress, a policy group that favors ending these taxes, says that ending this emergency “would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [UNN 3]

prerequisite_paths.reason: The taxes stop only because the emergency that supports them ends.

claims.title: A joint resolution is Congress's legal way to end an emergency
claims.statement: The National Emergencies Act lets Congress end a national emergency by enacting a joint resolution, and this bill uses that method.
claims.classification_reason: Direct statutory text; the bill itself cites the provision. Whether this emergency was unlawful or harmful is a different question and is not part of this statement.

claims.scope_html: This says only that the method exists and that this bill uses it. It does not say the emergency was illegal, or that ending it would bring a particular benefit.
claims.background_html: The President declares a national emergency. The law also gives Congress a way to end one. The Congressional Research Service, which writes reports for Congress, explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [UNC 24]

claims.statement: The April 2 order let the President raise these taxes further, including if another country retaliated or if U.S. manufacturing worsened. Ending the emergency ends that power under this order, but not tariff powers under other laws.

claims.title: The deals' tariff terms
claims.statement: The trade deals signed with Malaysia and Cambodia on October 26, 2025, and the framework with Thailand, set U.S. tax terms under this emergency alongside promises by those countries. They were not yet in force on October 30, 2025.
claims.classification_reason: Direct text of the agreements, the framework statement and the September order. No packet source disputes these terms. Whether the terms give pressure for the promises is a separate statement.
claims.scope_html: On October 30 these deals still needed further steps: “the United States and Malaysia will undertake domestic formalities in advance of the Agreement entering into force.” [UNT 10] Thailand had a framework only: the two countries “will negotiate and finalize the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade” [UNT 27]. Either side may end Malaysia's agreement: “Either Party may terminate this Agreement by written notification to the other Party.” [UNN 35]
claims.background_html: These deals are called Agreements on Reciprocal Trade. A framework is a plan for a later agreement. A party is a country in the agreement. The country's “domestic law” is its own law.
claims.support_html: In Malaysia's deal the United States will “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [UNC 26] and identify goods “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [UNC 26] The September order says relief depends on factors including “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [UNN 29]. Malaysia's enforcement article says: “If a Party considers that the other Party has not complied with a provision of this Agreement, the Party may review the terms of this Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [UNN 35] Cambodia's agreement has a similar article [UNN 36].

prerequisite_paths.reason: Direct text of the deals and the order; this step does not depend on any other claim.

claims.title: Tariff pressure behind the promises in the deals
claims.statement: Ending these taxes would remove an incentive and an enforcement tool for getting Malaysia and Cambodia to carry out the promises in their signed deals, including promises on market access, labor rights, the environment, security and supply, public rule-making and internet rules.
claims.classification_reason: Adequately sourced, and no retained response challenges this step. The April 2 order itself lists weak labor and environmental standards among the practices it addresses and allows lower rates if a partner remedies such practices. The September order ties relief to partners' commitments, and the deals contain these promises and allow action for not following 'a provision'. The Trade Representative says tariffs can go back into place. The remaining limits (not yet in force, no tariff action yet, general clause, other tools) do not deny that the tool existed on the comparison date. The response to SES_oppose_04 targets a later link and stays local.
claims.scope_html: The deals were signed but not in force on October 30, 2025. This statement concerns whether the tool existed on that date, not whether it had been used or how much it would achieve. The Trade Representative's own examples are “actually opening their market, [and] making the investment and purchase commitments they've agreed to.” [UNT 13] The enforcement article allows action “in accordance with applicable domestic law” [UNN 35] and does not name tariffs. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules set no product-level environmental conditions. Some promises are limited by their wording: Malaysia cooperates “in a manner consistent with applicable requirements of domestic laws and regulations” [SES 40], and its cyber clause says “may include” [SES 40]. The sources reviewed for this statement show no tariff action tied to one of these promises. Other U.S. trade laws also allow responses in some cases.
claims.background_html: Tariff relief means lowering these taxes on a country's goods. An incentive here means a reason for another government to act, because it wants lower U.S. taxes. An enforcement tool means a way to respond if a government breaks a promise. The U.S. Trade Representative is the U.S. official who leads trade talks.
claims.support_html:
The April 2 order lists among the practices it addresses “failures by governments in protecting labor and environment standards” [UNC 10] and “weak labor, environmental, and other regulatory standards and protections” [UNC 10]. It allows lower rates if a partner takes “significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters” [UNC 10]. The September order says earlier rate suspensions were “to reflect the fact that some trading partners had signaled a willingness to undertake meaningful economic and national security commitments with the United States” [SES 32].

The Malaysia statement lists promises in the same deal as the tariff terms: “Malaysia has committed to adopt and maintain high levels of environmental protection and to effectively enforce its environmental laws” [UNC 26] and “Malaysia has committed to refrain from banning, or imposing quotas on, exports to the United States of critical minerals or rare earth elements.” [UNC 26] The enforcement article applies if a country “has not complied with a provision of this Agreement” [UNN 35]. The Trade Representative said that if partners do not honor their agreements, “the president has his tariff authority,” [UNT 13] and that countries that do not comply “can have the tariffs go back into place.” [UNT 13] CNBC said it is not difficult to imagine that a country that agreed to buy goods “in order to avoid higher U.S. tariff rates might go back on that pledge” [UNT 13] if the court ruled against the tariffs.

prerequisite_paths.reason: The tool is removed only if the taxes stop, and it depends on the deals' tariff terms.

claims.title: Less uncertainty about tariff rates
claims.statement: Ending this emergency would make future U.S. tariff rates at least somewhat less uncertain and less subject to sudden change, even though other tariff powers would remain.
claims.classification_reason: Substantive objection to this exact statement: officials announced they would replace the tariffs under other laws, so uncertainty might only move. The evidence points in both directions and no packet source measures uncertainty after such a repeal.
claims.scope_html: This concerns policy expectations in the comparison used here, which is set on October 30, 2025. Later tariff events do not test what ending the emergency on that date would have done. The statement concerns whether uncertainty would fall, not by how much. What firms, markets or workers would do with less uncertainty is a later step in each reason.
claims.background_html: A tariff power is a legal authority to set tariffs. Section 122, Section 232 and Section 301 are other U.S. trade laws that allow tariffs under stated conditions.
claims.support_html: Ending the emergency removes this order's power to change rates. An October analysis says other laws “have more limits and/or procedural steps than IEEPA” [UNC 14], the emergency powers law. The Congressional Research Service says IEEPA, unlike other tariff laws, “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [UNC 24] Treasury Secretary Bessent called the other authorities “not as efficient, not as powerful” [SES 12].
claims.objection_html: Officials said the policy would continue another way. Trade adviser Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [UNC 13] Commerce Secretary Lutnick said: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [SES 11] An October 2025 analysis says other laws “could result in similar ends” [UNC 14]. So firms and markets could still face uncertainty about rates under other laws.

prerequisite_paths.reason: The uncertainty can fall only if this order's power to change rates ends.

claims.title: A matching cut by China
claims.statement: Ending the U.S. emergency taxes would make China more likely to lower the retaliatory charges it added on U.S. goods in response to them.
claims.classification_reason: Substantive objection already attached to UNN_support_05: the cited Chinese cut came from negotiation, a repeal would be one-sided, and China's decision is its own. UNC_support_04's easing route uses the same May negotiated example.
claims.scope_html: This concerns China's own charge in response to these taxes as it stood on October 30, 2025: a 10 percent charge, with 24 percent suspended. Other Chinese charges on U.S. goods have separate causes. The February 2026 Chinese statement came when replacement U.S. tariffs applied, so it does not test a one-sided repeal (ending the U.S. taxes without a negotiated exchange).
claims.background_html: Retaliatory charges are taxes a country adds on another country's goods in response to that country's taxes. The Chinese charge is decided by China, not by U.S. law.
claims.support_html: China tied its charge to the U.S. tax: “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [UNN 24]. China later “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” [UNN 25]. In February 2026, after U.S. Customs stopped collecting these taxes, China said it would decide “whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original U.S. fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs.” [UNN 28]
claims.objection_html: The cut came “following a U.S.-China economic and trade negotiation in Geneva” [UNN 25]. A repeal by Congress would be one-sided, not a negotiated exchange. A repeal does not change Chinese law. Other charges would remain: “certain U.S. agricultural products are also subject to Section 301 retaliatory tariffs” [UNN 25].

arguments.title: The bill lowers a cost barrier to replacing fossil fuels with less polluting power.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill lowers a cost barrier to replacing fossil fuels with less polluting power.

  • Because By September 2025, the basic import tax under this emergency had raised solar costs: “the baseline tariffs remained in effect and contributed to price increases across solar market segments” [5].
  • Because In April 2025, before the higher rate on China was suspended, an energy consultant listed imported storage and power equipment among the goods most affected: “Grid-scale batteries and solar panels, as well as power transformers, are among the hardest hit by price increases on imports” [6].
  • Because The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, warned in April 2025 that the taxes would also raise the cost of building clean energy factories, because the taxes apply to imported materials and equipment such as “cement, construction equipment” [7].
  • So Ending these extra taxes reduces a cost barrier to installing clean power and to building clean energy factories.
  • Because Storage helps clean power replace fossil fuels: “Batteries allow renewables to replace fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal, while keeping a steady flow of power when sources like wind and solar are not producing.” [6]
  • Because Fossil fuel pollution harms plants and animals: “SO 2 causes acid rain, which is harmful to plants and to animals that live in water.” [8] SO 2 is sulfur dioxide, a gas released when fossil fuels are burned.
  • Because Burning fossil fuels also heats the planet: “Burning oil and gas emits greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, which trap heat in the atmosphere and warm the planet” [9].
  • Because Warming damages natural areas on land, in water and around ice. The U.N. climate science panel finds: “Climate change has caused substantial damages, and increasingly irreversible losses, in terrestrial, freshwater, cryospheric, and coastal and open ocean ecosystems (high confidence).” [10]
  • So Making it easier to replace fossil fuels with clean power supports [NAME]'s goal of protecting nature from air pollution and warming.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: By the bill date (October 30, 2025), the higher reciprocal tariff rate on China was suspended through November 10, 2025. A 55% battery price estimate in an April 2025 AP news article applied "if the tariffs are fully implemented on China." Sources: [11], [6].

Evidence note: An October 2025 Wood Mackenzie report calls two kinds of large electrical equipment, generation step-up transformers and power transformers, the biggest bottlenecks (the items that slow projects most), with delivery times measured in years. The report says transformer prices have stabilised. It describes tariffs as driving up costs and extending timelines. Sources: [12].

Evidence note: In an April 2025 AP news article, experts said a trade slowdown might bring a brief and slight reduction in greenhouse gases: at most about 1% if full tariffs were implemented. The experts also said harm to clean energy would outweigh this reduction. Sources: [6].

arguments.title: The bill eases the cost pressure on water treatment and reuse projects that protect rivers and habitats.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill eases the cost pressure on water treatment and reuse projects that protect rivers and habitats.

  • Because An April water-industry report said utilities (the organizations that supply water) import pumps, membranes and treatment supplies: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities.” [15]
  • Because Higher costs can delay treatment work. In May 2025, when Chinese goods faced a 145% rate that was later suspended, the city of Decatur, Arkansas, had received part of its water treatment supplies and was postponing the purchase of the rest: “it will wait as long as possible for the rest, until the tariff issue is resolved” [16].
  • Because An April 2025 industry warning said water reuse projects also depend on equipment exposed to these taxes: “Membrane-based reuse and desalination systems—already under pressure in California, Texas, Florida—are particularly exposed.” [17]
  • Because Water reuse treats polluted water: “This practice reduces pollutant discharges, such as nutrients, while increasing the reliability of community water supplies.” [18]
  • Because Water reuse also supplies water for wildlife: “Water reuse can help restore ecosystems by providing them with a consistent water source.” [18]
  • So Removing these extra taxes from treatment equipment leaves more project money for cleaning water and sustaining habitats. Both serve [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.

arguments.title: The bill makes expanding recycling less costly.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill makes expanding recycling less costly.

  • Because Recycling relies on imported machinery: “Most of the sectors’ equipment comes from overseas, and high tariffs could hinder domestic recycling infrastructure buildout and rattle commodities markets.” [20]
  • Because A July 2025 industry report identified a tax on recycling equipment from Europe: “Today they are subject to a 10 percent duty” [20]. Here, “they” means equipment imported from the European Union, and a duty is an import tax.
  • Because The later tariff framework between the United States and the European Union (EU) still included “a reciprocal tariff” [21]. “Reciprocal tariff” is the name for the taxes under this emergency.
  • Because Recycling protects nature: “Recycling benefits the environment by reducing the amount of waste sent to landfills and incinerators, conserving natural resources and preventing pollution.” [22]
  • So Ending the emergency tax on recycling machinery covered by that tax lowers a barrier to expanding this work. Conserving resources and preventing waste give [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

arguments.title: The bill removes a U.S. source of tariff conflict that threatens Brazilian forests and savannas.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 The bill removes a U.S. source of tariff conflict that threatens Brazilian forests and savannas.

  • Because China imposed an extra tax in response to the April policy: “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [24]. IEEPA is the emergency powers law used for these taxes.
  • Because That April retaliation still applied when the Senate voted. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) records an extension “for another 90 days from August 12, 2025, while retaining the 10 percent tariff” [25].
  • Because China's charge has moved with U.S.-China talks. After negotiations in Geneva, it “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” [25] charge.
  • Because The emergency also allows further U.S. tariff increases in response to retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order” [26]. The HTSUS is the official U.S. list of import tax rates.
  • Because After the May 2025 tariff reductions, the research group Trase still identified a threat to Brazilian habitats: “there remains a risk that the surge in demand for Brazilian soy from China, resulting from the ongoing tensions, could increase deforestation and carbon emissions in Brazil.” [27]
  • So Ending the U.S. taxes behind that retaliation, and their possible increase under this emergency, removes one source of a trade conflict that puts habitats at risk. arguments.title: The bill takes away emergency tariff pressure aimed at weakening environmental rules.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 The bill takes away emergency tariff pressure aimed at weakening environmental rules.

  • Because The September 2025 order tied tariff relief to “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [29].
  • Because The EU tariff framework called for changes to companies' climate obligations: “to propose changes to the requirement for a harmonised civil liability regime for due diligence failures and to climate-transition-related obligations.” [21] A civil liability regime is a set of rules that lets people bring legal claims against companies. Due diligence means checking for harm in a company's supply chain.

  • So Ending the emergency takes away its import taxes as a tool for these demands. Defending rules against climate pollution and damage in supply chains serves [NAME]'s commitment to defend nature.

arguments.title: The bill removes emergency tariff pressure for energy purchases that add climate pollution.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The bill removes emergency tariff pressure for energy purchases that add climate pollution.

  • Because The EU tariff framework includes an energy purchase plan: “the European Union intends to procure US liquified natural gas, oil, and nuclear energy products” [21].
  • Because In August 2025, a trade analyst explained the continuing tariff pressure: “The key to keeping the EU-US trade deal on track will be demonstrating rising EU energy purchases and investments in the US” [32].
  • Because The gas purchases have a pollution cost even when they replace gas delivered by pipeline. Chatham House researcher Chris Aylett explained: “Swapping pipeline gas for American LNG would further increase Europe's emissions” [9]. LNG means gas cooled into liquid for shipping.
  • Because The source explains why: “That's because LNG production and transport emits more methane — a greenhouse gas far more potent than CO2, though it doesn't stay as long in the atmosphere.” [9]
  • Because Human-caused climate change already causes “widespread adverse impacts and related losses and damages to nature and people” [10].
  • So Ending this emergency removes its tariff pressure to expand purchases with those pollution costs. Resisting that pressure gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill as a way to defend nature from climate harm.
arguments.con_html:
Response The EU's energy purchase pledge does not establish the extra switch from pipeline gas to U.S. shipped gas that this Point's pollution claim needs.

  • Because LNG analyst Youri Leconte describes the U.S.-EU deal as a continuation of an existing market shift: “This deal is more of a rebranding of positions that were already emerging due to the market shifts post-2022” [33].
  • Because The same report identifies who controls purchases: “Goldwyn said the commercial terms of any forthcoming contracts will still have to be competitive since the EU cannot compel European utilities to purchase US energy.” [33]
  • Because This Point's emissions comparison concerns one particular replacement: “Swapping pipeline gas for American LNG would further increase Europe's emissions” [9]. LNG is gas cooled into liquid for shipping.
  • So This Point needs to connect this emergency's pressure to purchases beyond those that existing markets would bring, including a change from pipeline gas to shipped gas. The pledge and the pollution comparison do not establish that change. So they do not establish pollution this repeal would avoid.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The DW article reports an EU Commission spokesperson saying the deal would have no impact on EU decarbonization targets. CNBC reports analysts doubt the $750 billion pledge is feasible. S&P quotes an analyst calling the deal a very positive signal for U.S. LNG. Sources: [9], [32], [33].

arguments.title: The bill removes tariff pressure for stronger protection against illegal logging.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes tariff pressure for stronger protection against illegal logging.

  • Because In its trade deal with the United States, Cambodia promises action against illegal timber trade: “Cambodia shall take measures to combat, and cooperate with the United States to prevent, trade in illegally harvested forest products.” [37]
  • Because Cambodia also promises stronger enforcement: “Cambodia shall fully implement existing laws and regulations for forest sector governance, including anti-corruption measures, and strengthen institutions responsible for enforcing these laws.” [37]
  • Because In its deal, Malaysia promises independent oversight of timber permits: “establish or uphold an independent forestry oversight body to supervise timber concessions and permits” [35].
  • So These promises support care for forests through checks on cutting trees and stronger enforcement. Ending the tariffs behind these promises weakens an incentive for those protections. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Section 301, a separate U.S. trade law, lets the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency, respond to trade agreement violations, generally after consulting the foreign country. In July 2025 USTR opened an investigation of Brazil that included illegal deforestation; no finding or penalty appears in this source. Sources: [38], [39].

Evidence note: Five reasons against S.J.Res.88 about protecting nature share one causal step: tariffs under this emergency work as an incentive and enforcement tool. These five reasons concern illegal logging, illegal trade in wild animals and plants, overfishing, careful use of materials, and a public process for defending nature. This reason is one of them. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules cap the rate at 19 percent and exempt listed goods. The schedules set no environmental conditions for individual products. The enforcement clause says a party (a country in the agreement) may act "in accordance with applicable domestic law." Both agreements were still waiting to take effect on the bill date (October 30, 2025). Sources: [36], [35].

Brief context note: The 2026 Trade Policy Agenda (March 2026) comes from the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency. The agenda lists labor and environmental standards and national and economic security among the commitments in Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ARTs), which are trade deals. It describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff (an added tariff above the normal rate). USTR says courts can review the tools for maintaining those tariffs and that those tools may change. USTR also says it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. The agenda reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result. It also does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [40].

Brief context note: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the United States but had not ratified it (given it final legal approval). The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [41].

Point 6 The bill removes a price restraint on clothing purchases and the environmental harm tied to them.

  • Because The vice president of Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers’ association reported lower clothing demand after the new tax under this emergency, called the reciprocal tariff: “US consumer spending has slowed due to the high tariff.   • Because Clothing producers reported fewer orders because of the reciprocal tax itself. The president of Bangladesh’s knitwear producers’ association said: “Due to the reciprocal tariff, US buyers are delaying or reducing orders as they negotiate to shift part of the tariff burden onto Bangladeshi suppliers.” [44]
  • So Ending this extra import cost removes a restraint on orders for new clothing.
  • Because Making short-lived clothing and throwing it away harms nature. The U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) explains: “These clothes are often worn for only a short time, then jettisoned into landfills or incinerated. This feeds climate change, depletes natural resources and floods land, sea and air with hazardous chemicals.” [45]

  • So The bill gives up a tax that holds back purchases of new clothing. New clothing creates demand for production, materials, water, transport and waste disposal. [NAME]’s wish to protect nature from destruction and pollution gives a reason to oppose losing that restraint.

arguments.pro_html:

arguments.title: Ending the emergency, a source of sudden import tax changes, protects access to jobs and safe work.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Ending the emergency, a source of sudden import tax changes, protects access to jobs and safe work.

  • Because The April 2 order allows further tax rises, including power to “increase duties under this order” [10].
  • Because Uncertainty about tariff rates holds back staffing. In its June 2025 survey of firms in the Fourth Federal Reserve District (a region served by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland), the Cleveland Fed found that “19 percent of contacts said that tariff-related uncertainty had led their firm to scale back staffing plans” [11].
  • Because Uncertainty also threatens workers' protection abroad. Asked about tariff uncertainty, Sara Park of the International Labour Organization (ILO) explained: “During periods of crisis or uncertainty, investment generally pauses. One concern is that factories stop investing in improving working conditions, which could affect occupational safety and health.” [12]
  • So Ending the emergency removes its power to change these tax rates again. That removes a source of pressure to hold back hiring and safety improvements. Protecting opportunities to find paid work and stay safe at work serves [NAME]'s concern for workers, including vulnerable workers abroad.
arguments.con_html:
Response Closing one legal way of making sudden tax changes does not establish less uncertainty about the rates firms would actually pay. This response does not deny that the bill ends this order's own power to raise rates.

  • Because Replacement plans were announced before the vote. In a May interview transcribed in a June 2 court filing, trade adviser Peter Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [13] Here, “lose” means lose in court. This was a stated plan to keep the tariff policy after losing its emergency-law basis.
  • Because An October 2025 analysis described a possible temporary step toward other tariff powers: “Five months of Section 122 tariffs would provide time for the Commerce Department to do the investigation required by Section 232 of the Trade Act of 1962 for a president to impose tariffs for national security reasons.” [14] Using Section 122 would still have to meet the conditions in that law.
  • So Hiring and safety plans respond to uncertainty about future rates, whichever law sets them. Given the announced search for replacement powers, this Point's evidence does not establish that ending this legal way of setting tariffs would make rates more predictable.

arguments.title: Removing these import taxes, a proven trigger for retaliation by other countries, reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Removing these import taxes, a proven trigger for retaliation by other countries, reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.

  • Because China directly answered the April taxes with taxes on U.S. exports. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, says that “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [15].
  • Because Retaliation puts sellers at a disadvantage: “Foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports make U.S. goods less competitive in foreign markets compared to goods not subject to tariffs” [15]. October reporting shows what this can mean for farm income: one Minnesota grower was selling soybeans “for less than what it cost to produce them.” [16]
  • Because Reducing the U.S. taxes has already helped ease this conflict. The May 2025 joint agreement paired U.S. tariff cuts with China's commitment to “suspend or remove the non-tariff countermeasures taken against the United States since April 2, 2025.” [17] Non-tariff countermeasures are responses other than taxes on goods.
  • So Ending these taxes and their power to fuel new rounds of retaliation reduces an avoidable risk to export sales. Protecting people whose livelihoods are caught in that conflict gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: China's March 2025 farm duties responded to a U.S. action separate from the April 2 emergency. On October 30, 2025, China said the U.S. would suspend the 24 percent reciprocal tariff for another year and that China would adjust its countermeasures, and reported consensus on expanding agricultural trade. The May 2025 deal left China's 10 percent charge in place. Sources: [15], [18], [17].

Evidence note: By February 26, 2026, U.S. Customs had stopped collecting tariffs under IEEPA (the emergency powers law) and had begun a surcharge, or added tax, under Section 122, another trade law. On that date, China's commerce ministry said it would assess those measures and then decide whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs. The ministry also noted U.S. statements about tariffs through investigations under Section 301 and Section 232, two other trade laws. This is an official position, not a final tariff adjustment. Because replacement tariffs applied, this statement is not a test of a one-sided repeal in October 2025. Sources: [19].

arguments.title: Removing import taxes on poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Removing import taxes on poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.

  • Because The reciprocal taxes threaten demand for these workers' goods. The October clothing study warns that “the elevated tariffs are set to reduce demand, squeeze suppliers, and depress investment in future capacity” [4].
  • Because This reaches an important source of women's earnings. UN Trade and Development's October 30 report states: “The textile and apparel industry, an important source of employment for women in many LDCs, has been hit hardest.” [20] LDCs are countries the U.N. classifies as least developed.
  • Because Workers can have few other ways to earn a living. The Fuller Project reports: “Women in Lesotho, Bangladesh and Cambodia all said there were no realistic employment alternatives available to them.” [21] A worker-rights researcher warns that if these jobs go, “workers will struggle to pay for basic necessities such as food, school fees, and healthcare” [21].
  • Because Lost sales and investment also threaten future opportunities. The U.N. report warns: “Higher levels of US protection on manufacturing, agriculture and food risk dampening LDCs’ hard-won progress in building productive capacities, reducing commodity dependence and promoting value addition.” [20] That means building the ability to make more goods, sell a wider range of products and do more of the work that adds to their value.
  • So Removing the added tax supports demand for workers' goods and investment in future production. That protects earnings for food, schooling and healthcare, women's ability to earn, and poorer countries' paths to better work. These are reasons for [NAME], who values protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.

arguments.title: Ending this emergency’s import taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 Ending this emergency’s import taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.

  • Because The emergency's stated problem is reflected in “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [10]. A trade deficit means the United States buys more goods from abroad than it sells abroad.
  • Because Small, poor economies have little ability to buy U.S. goods. The U.N. explains: “As many of these economies are small in size, structurally weak with low purchasing power, they offer limited export market opportunities for the US.” [22]
  • Because Lesotho shows the mismatch. Its share of the U.S. goods trade deficit in the U.N.'s 2024 data was tiny: “Lesotho 0.019%” [23]. Lesotho still faced an added tax under the later rates. September 2025 reporting describes “a much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21].
  • So Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people whose countries have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Fair treatment calls for burdens to reflect people's circumstances and their part in the problem. Sparing poor people this disproportionate burden serves [NAME]'s concern for justice across borders.
arguments.con_html:
Response The deficit-share comparison does not establish the unfair treatment it is used to prove.

  • Because The U.N.'s “Lesotho 0.019%” [23] measures a country’s share of the total U.S. goods trade deficit. The reported “much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21] measures a tax on the value of covered imports. Neither percentage measures the tax cost compared with a poor person’s income.
  • Because This Point adds a rule that the burden is unjust because the country contributes little to the total deficit. [NAME]’s concern for just treatment of people does not by itself establish that national trade shares determine the burdens individuals should bear.
  • So A small country’s small share of a large country’s deficit is not a measure of injustice to its workers. The two percentages do not support the claimed disproportionate burden or show that ending it would correct unjust treatment.

Point 7 Ending this use of emergency power limits burdens imposed without the investigation other tariff laws usually require.

  • Because The emergency powers law, called IEEPA, skips a check found in other main tariff laws. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, explains that it “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [24]

  • Because This bill makes Congress's power to end that use of emergency authority effective. CRS explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [24]
  • So People whose food budgets and jobs are at stake deserve public review of burdens placed on them. Ending this emergency enforces Congress's check on a way of taxing that does not require an investigation. That supports [NAME]'s concern that everyone be treated justly.

arguments.title: The bill removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.

  • Because The president of Unionwear, a U.S. maker, explains the price protection: “Each tariff increase reduces the cost advantage of imports, making our domestic production more competitive without us having to change anything.” [27] He also explains why taxes on the firm’s supplies do little to offset that benefit: “We source our raw materials domestically when possible, so tariffs on finished goods help us while tariffs on materials have minimal impact on our cost structure.” [27]
  • Because U.S. makers have reported winning work. Royal Apparel said: “Several production programs that were initially set to go overseas have now been redirected to Royal Apparel” [28].
  • Because This demand reaches employers that open doors to people with disabilities. The cofounder of Stakes Manufacturing said its April garment partnership would “meet the rising demand driven by recent tariff changes” [28]. Reporting on the firm found: “10% of the 225 employees at Stakes Manufacturing are people with an intellectual or developmental disability.” [29]
  • Because Earlier import shocks (sudden rises in imports) from China trade do not measure the effect of this change. They do show how hard lost factory work can be to replace for people without degrees: “Almost all of the manufacturing job losses affected workers without a college degree, and this group saw almost no job gains in the next two decades.” [30]
  • Because Those earlier import shocks also harmed children through their parents’ lost earnings. A study of trade shocks to young men’s relative earnings (their pay compared with women’s) found that “these shocks heighten male idleness and premature mortality, and raise the share of mothers who are unwed and the share of children living in below-poverty, single-headed households.” [31]
  • So Removing this price protection puts vulnerable workers’ opportunities and their families’ security at risk. Protecting people who face barriers to work, and children who bear the costs of lost work, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Import taxes under Executive Order 14257 are added to other import taxes that the bill leaves in place. The redirected orders concern Royal Apparel and the disability-employment figure concerns Stakes; the Stakes statement refers to recent tariff changes generally. The Autor, Dorn and Hanson study period is 1990-2014. Sources: [10], [28], [29], [31].

Evidence note: The researchers Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. The researchers Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases lost jobs compared with less exposed industries. A positive protection effect was offset by input costs (the cost of materials and parts) and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [32], [33].

Brief context note: The 2026 Trade Policy Agenda (March 2026) comes from the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency. The agenda lists labor and environmental standards and national and economic security among the commitments in Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ARTs), which are trade deals. It describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff (an added tariff above the normal rate). USTR says courts can review the tools for maintaining those tariffs and that those tools may change. USTR also says it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. The agenda reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result. It also does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [34].

Brief context note: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the United States but had not ratified it (given it final legal approval). The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [35].

arguments.title: The bill removes a way to press governments to stop treating people’s work unfairly because it comes from abroad.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill removes a way to press governments to stop treating people’s work unfairly because it comes from abroad.

  • Because In its signed trade deal with the United States, Cambodia promises equal access for farm goods: “Cambodia shall provide non-discriminatory market access for U.S. agricultural goods as set forth in this Agreement.” [36]
  • Because The deal also protects people selling services against worse treatment than local or other foreign sellers: “Cambodia shall refrain from imposing new barriers that provide less favorable treatment to U.S. services suppliers than the treatment afforded to domestic services suppliers and services suppliers from any third country, jurisdiction, or economy.” [36]
  • Because More talks to remove barriers were underway: “President Trump remains in active negotiations with many countries to further eliminate barriers to U.S. exports.” [37]
  • So The bill removes these U.S. import taxes without requiring governments to agree to or carry out such changes. That removes an incentive to end discrimination that limits people’s chances to earn a living. Equal opportunities and just treatment give [NAME] a reason to oppose.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Five reasons against S.J.Res.88 about concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment share one incentive step (tariffs giving other governments a reason to act) and are not independent evidence for that step. These five reasons concern fair treatment of work from abroad, Malaysia’s ban on imports made with forced labor, workplace protections abroad, fishing safeguards, and a source of materials for medical tools. This reason is one of them. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules cap the Executive Order 14257 rate at 19 percent. Section 301, a separate U.S. trade law, allows tariffs after findings and procedures when a country denies agreement rights or fails to enforce commitments concerning labor and the environment. original.title: It removes tariff pressure to carry out basic workplace protections abroad.
original.pro_html:
Point 4 It removes tariff pressure to carry out basic workplace protections abroad.

  • Because Cambodia’s signed agreement requires labor-law enforcement: “Cambodia shall establish and effectively apply appropriate legal sanctions for violations of those laws.” [36]
  • Because The rights covered include “a prohibition on the worst forms of child labor; and acceptable conditions of work with respect to minimum wages and hours of work.” [36]
  • Because Broken commitments permit a response under domestic law: “the Party may review the terms of the Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [36]
  • So Ending this emergency removes a tariff tool for pressing Cambodia to carry out those promises. Protecting children from the worst forms of labor, and workers from abuse over pay and hours, directly serves [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people abroad.

arguments.title: The bill weakens pressure for fishing safeguards that protect coastal families’ food and income.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 The bill weakens pressure for fishing safeguards that protect coastal families’ food and income.

  • Because Malaysia’s deal includes concrete environmental promises: “Malaysia has committed to adopt and maintain high levels of environmental protection and to effectively enforce its environmental laws, including by taking measures to address illegal logging, fisheries subsidies, illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, and illegal wildlife trade.” [26]
  • Because The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization explains the human stakes of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing: “This global threat undermines the health of marine ecosystems, jeopardizes food security, and threatens the livelihoods of millions, particularly small-scale fishers.” [42]
  • So Ending the tariffs behind these promises weakens a way to press for enforcement that protects these families’ food and work. Protecting vulnerable people who depend on shared fishing grounds gives [NAME] a reason to oppose.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Five reasons against S.J.Res.88 about concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment share one incentive step (tariffs giving other governments a reason to act) and are not independent evidence for that step. These five reasons concern fair treatment of work from abroad, Malaysia’s ban on imports made with forced labor, workplace protections abroad, fishing safeguards, and a source of materials for medical tools. This reason is one of them. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules cap the Executive Order 14257 rate at 19 percent. Section 301, a separate U.S. trade law, allows tariffs after findings and procedures when a country denies agreement rights or fails to enforce commitments concerning labor and the environment. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. The agenda reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result. It also does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [34].

arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The bill removes a demonstrated means of pressing Thailand and Cambodia to keep the peace.

  • Because Reuters reports a role for trade pressure in ending the July fighting: “Trump helped broker an end to the five-day conflict in July by calling the then-leaders of the two countries and urging them to end hostilities or risk their respective trade talks with Washington being put on hold.” [46]
  • Because Reuters’ account of the July truce links talks to the tariff threat: “Washington would not move ahead with tariff negotiations with both until the conflict had ended.” [47] The account also records the reward: “Mr Trump said tariff negotiations with both countries resumed after the ceasefire agreement.” [47]

  • Because The July fighting had “killed at least 48 people and temporarily displaced an estimated 300,000” [46].
  • So Ending this emergency’s tariff power removes an incentive already used to bring the two countries toward a truce and to keep trade tied to peace. Protecting border communities from renewed killing and displacement gives [NAME] a reason to oppose.

arguments.title: The bill helps people keep their food traditions and the shared places where others can learn about them.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill helps people keep their food traditions and the shared places where others can learn about them.

  • Because Tariff costs were still reaching cultural grocery stores in October 2025. At Chicago’s 88 Marketplace, the manager said “the recent 15% import tariffs on South Korean products will make it harder for the grocer to keep prices down.” [6]
  • Because Customers were already paying some of those costs, according to Jan Zhu, the store manager: “While the store is absorbing some of the price increases, Zhu said it has still been forced to pass along some cost hikes to customers.” [6]
  • Because Local replacements are hard to find: “And often, these items, like grains, spices or herbs, are not easily sourced in the U.S.” [6]
  • Because These foods support cultural practices: “Food is an important way Asian Americans take part in their culture.” [7]
  • So Ending this added tax removes a cost that makes familiar foods harder to stock and afford. Helping neighbors keep their own food traditions puts acceptance of different ways of life into practice.
  • Because The stores also provide places for people from different backgrounds to meet. Reporting on Chicago’s Gangnam Market explains: “The store hosts different activities, including mahjong games, K-pop dance performances and anime exhibitions, for all ages and backgrounds.” [8]
  • So The same tax relief helps keep open shared spaces for meeting people and learning about their cultures. [NAME]’s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a further reason to protect these opportunities.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: In the October Sun-Times report, the 88 Marketplace manager says tariffs were not as high as in April and May and describes supply shortages. A December Medill report says inflation and tariffs together threaten these supermarkets. Sources: [6], [8].

arguments.title: The bill removes part of a trade conflict that puts Asian Americans at risk of blame for another country’s actions.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill removes part of a trade conflict that puts Asian Americans at risk of blame for another country’s actions.

  • Because This tariff program allows higher taxes in response to another country’s retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [3]

arguments.title: The bill weakens pressure against excluding workers because of their identity or beliefs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill weakens pressure against excluding workers because of their identity or beliefs.

  • Because Both trade deals require protection of basic labor rights: “Malaysia shall protect internationally recognized labor rights.” [12] “Cambodia shall protect internationally recognized labor rights.” [14]
  • Because Malaysia's agreement defines those rights to include “the International Labor Organization (ILO) Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and its Follow-Up (1998), as amended in 2022” [12].
  • Because The declaration includes “the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation” [15].
  • Because The ILO's discrimination standard names “race, colour, sex, religion, political opinion, national extraction or social origin” [16].
  • So Tariff pressure backs a promise to protect people at work despite differences in origin, faith or political views.
  • So [NAME]'s commitment to accepting different people gives a reason to oppose removing that pressure.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Brief context note: Section 301, a separate U.S. trade law, covers denial of U.S. rights under a trade agreement and persistent failure to enforce commitments on labor and the environment, including tariff responses after required findings. In October 2025 the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency, proposed duties on Nicaragua over labor abuses. It also opened an investigation into how China carried out the Phase One trade agreement. Neither action was yet an imposed penalty. Sources: [17], [18], [19].

Evidence note: The reasons against S.J.Res.88 about accepting people who are different share one tariff-pressure step (U.S. tariffs used to press other governments). This reason is one of them. In August 2025, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said deals would "stick regardless of what happens in litigation" and described deals as premised on opening markets and on investment and purchase commitments; CNBC said it was not hard to imagine partners going back on pledges if the courts ruled against the tariffs. Sources: [13].

Brief context note: The 2026 Trade Policy Agenda (March 2026) comes from the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency. The agenda lists labor and environmental standards and national and economic security among the commitments in Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ARTs), which are trade deals. It describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff (an added tariff above the normal rate). USTR says courts can review the tools for maintaining those tariffs and that those tools may change. USTR also says it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. The agenda reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result. It also does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [20].

Brief context note: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the United States but had not ratified it (given it final legal approval). The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [21].

Evidence note: The September 2025 tariff order makes relief depend on numerous factors, including the scope and economic value of a partner's commitments. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer's August 2025 examples were commercial: opening markets and making investment and purchase commitments. He also said that if partners do not honor their agreements, the President has his tariff authority. The Malaysia agreement's general clause lets a party take action under domestic law if it considers a provision breached. The sources reviewed show no tariff action tied to a labor provision. Sources: [11], [13], [12].

arguments.title: The bill weakens pressure to let migrant workers represent their co-workers.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill weakens pressure to let migrant workers represent their co-workers.

  • Because Within two years of the trade agreement taking effect, Malaysia must “amend its Trade Unions Act 1959 [Act 262] to allow migrant workers to hold elected union office without prior authorization” [22]. A union is a workers' organization.
  • So The reform removes an extra permission requirement for foreign workers to become elected union representatives. This lets people from outside the country speak and lead.
  • So [NAME]'s commitment to accepting different groups gives a reason to oppose removing tariff pressure for this inclusion.

  • So [NAME]'s wish to listen to different views and accept disagreement supports keeping tariff pressure behind those protections.

original.title: It removes tariff pressure supporting dialogue and mutual respect between Thailand and Cambodia.
original.pro_html:
Point 8 It removes tariff pressure supporting dialogue and mutual respect between Thailand and Cambodia.

  • Because Tariff pressure helped bring Thailand to the July talks: “President Trump’s threat to halt tariff talks has forced Thailand’s hand.” [30]
  • Because The connection continued at the October 26 signing. Trump said: “We do transactions, lots of them, with both nations as long as they live in peace” [31].
  • Because Thailand's framework still offered relief under the same tariff order: “the reciprocal tariffs, as set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [27].
  • Because A final deal remained ahead: “In the coming weeks, the United States and Thailand will negotiate and finalize the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade” [27].
  • Because The October 26 declaration requires both governments to “Refrain from disseminating or promoting false information, accusations, allegations, and harmful rhetoric” [32] to “mitigate negative public sentiment, and foster an environment conducive to peaceful dialogue.” [32]
  • Because They also commit to “resolve differences peacefully, in the spirit of good neighborliness, friendship, and solidarity” [32].
  • So Continued tariff bargaining supplied pressure for rivals to maintain dialogue and curb hostility toward the other national group. The bill removes that pressure while the trade deal and these steps still require follow-through.
  • So [NAME]'s wish to understand different people and accept disagreement gives a reason to preserve pressure for those practices.

arguments.title: Ending this emergency’s import taxes removes a threat to safe treatment and infection control.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Ending this emergency’s import taxes removes a threat to safe treatment and infection control.

  • Because Hospitals use imported essentials: “These imports include many low-margin, high-use essentials in hospital settings necessary for patient care.” [5]
  • Because Replacing suppliers can take years: “Manufacturers cannot easily pivot to new suppliers, absent multi-year lead times” [3].
  • Because Taxes can make supplies harder to obtain: “Tariffs also may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” [5] Vendors are sellers.
  • Because Missing devices threaten patients: “Disruption in the availability of these devices would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” [5].
  • So Removing this added burden helps keep supplies available for surgery and infection control when [NAME] needs care.

arguments.title: Lower medical costs help people get needed care.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Lower medical costs help people get needed care.

  • Because Higher hospital costs can reach patients through insurance charges and bills: “This would result in downstream cost shifting to patients through increased premiums, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket expenses.” [6] Premiums and deductibles are amounts people pay for health insurance and before insurance pays.
  • Because Cost already blocks care. The same article reports people “delaying or skipping care due to cost.” [6]
  • So Removing these taxes eases pressure on medical bills and insurance costs. This helps [NAME] obtain care that protects their health.
arguments.con_html:
Response Lower hospital supply costs do not establish the lower patient charges on which this care-access argument depends. This response does not settle what happens when contracts and premiums are reset.

  • Because The sentence about higher patient charges follows a conditional step: “In the near term, financial pressures could incentivize hospitals to seek higher reimbursement rates from insurers.” [6]
  • Because The hospital association’s October 17 letter explains who bears costs under existing payment rules: “Given that hospital payments are set by government and private payer contracts, the costs would be borne by hospitals directly.” [7]
  • So A tax saving does not itself change an agreed payment rate. This Point does not establish how savings would reach patients through lower bills, premiums or deductibles and improve access to care.

arguments.title: Lower supply costs help hospitals and ambulance services keep staff, services, and reliable equipment.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Lower supply costs help hospitals and ambulance services keep staff, services, and reliable equipment.

  • Because Supply costs compete with care budgets: “Rising supply costs force budget reallocation, limiting investment in staff, technology, and patient care.” [8]
  • Because The hospital association cites a survey, taken in January 2025 before the April emergency, in which administrators expected to “delay equipment upgrades to manage financial strain.” [5]
  • Because Equipment quality matters for finding illness. One surveyed administrator explains: “We do not want to misdiagnose a patient because we have decided to use lower quality equipment that cannot detect their issue.” [8]
  • Because Ambulance services also depend on imports. In April 2025, their association warned about imported supplies and medicines. Medicines were exempt from these taxes. The association wrote: “Tariffs on any of these items will increase prices, and could result in product shortages, additional supply chain complexity, and other challenges that EMS simply cannot afford.” [9] EMS means emergency medical services.
  • So Removing taxes on covered supplies eases pressure to cut staff, services or equipment spending. That protects [NAME]’s access to emergency help and accurate diagnosis.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.

Evidence note: The letter from the National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT) dates from April 2025. It cites persistent low payment for emergency medical services (EMS) and asks the Administration to consider EMS impacts of additional tariff actions. Sources: [9].

It reports that the survey was conducted in late January 2025, before the April emergency, and that it covered tariffs on Chinese imports, including expected medicine costs. Sources: [10].

arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Ending this emergency’s import taxes protects research on better ways to prevent and treat disease.

  • Because Disease research needs imports that a Johns Hopkins report described in April 2025 as taxed: “Biomedical labs rely heavily on imported equipment and materials, from microscopes to diagnostic tools, much of which is now subject to steep tariffs.” [11]

  • Because Medical device makers also face pressure on research and development, meaning work on new or better products: “U.S. companies have been shifting resources to manage tariff costs, with R&D spending expected to be the most heavily impacted.” [3]
  • Because That research serves patients. The industry describes its focus as “patient-centered diagnostics and treatments” [3], meaning ways to find and treat illness.
  • So Removing these costs protects the research that better tests and treatments depend on. This advances [NAME]’s goal of avoiding and overcoming disease.

arguments.title: Lower food costs help protect a diet that prevents disease.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Lower food costs help protect a diet that prevents disease.

  • Because Nutritious imports remained taxed in late October. An October 24 report confirmed that major banana suppliers remained covered by the tax. An economist explained that “we absolutely should expect a 10% tax on banana imports to drive banana prices higher” [14].
  • Because Higher prices can worsen diets: “During periods of rising prices or uncertainty, households often shift from perishable nutritious foods towards cheaper, longer lasting processed items, reducing the overall quality of the diet.” [15]
  • Because The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the U.S. public health agency, explains why fruits and vegetables matter: “they contribute important nutrients, can reduce the risk for many chronic diseases, and can also help with weight management.” [16]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers a barrier to nutritious food. This helps [NAME] protect their health.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: CNBC reports bananas up 5.4% since April, without measuring consumption. A commentary in the medical journal BMJ says tariffs may raise both healthy and unhealthy food costs and fall most on lower-income households. Sources: [14], [15].

arguments.title: The bill removes support for U.S. medical-supply factories that provide a backup during health emergencies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes support for U.S. medical-supply factories that provide a backup during health emergencies.

  • Because The taxes under this emergency cover medical gloves from suppliers beyond China. For rubber surgical gloves, an October 9 analysis records a “19% tariff on those from Malaysia” [32]. The October 26 Malaysia agreement keeps “at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025” [33].
  • Because U.S. medical-supply makers explain the link to emergency production: “Reciprocal tariffs aren’t just about fairness; they’re about ensuring that our nation can produce life-saving medical supplies when they matter most.” [34]
  • Because Reliable supplies protect patients and the public. The U.S. health department says protective gear and medical equipment “serve vital roles in protecting patients, healthcare workers, and the public.” [35] It also identifies the need to keep U.S. suppliers in business: “the U.S. Government has a vested interest in U.S. companies' continued marketplace viability” [35].
  • So Ending the tax removes a price advantage for U.S.-made gloves and removes support for keeping that production available when overseas supplies are disrupted.
  • So [NAME] needs protection from infection and safe medical care. Keeping that backup supply gives [NAME] a personal health reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html:
Response This Point's price advantage does not establish that these emergency taxes keep medical backup production available. This response does not deny that the tax gives U.S.-made gloves some price advantage over Malaysian gloves.

  • Because A U.S. glove maker's restart was linked to taxes on China: “new U.S. tariffs on rubber gloves from China have doubled the price from a few months ago” [36]; “SafeSource restarted two production lines to accommodate recent new orders” [36].
  • Because The bill targets “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025” [1]. China’s separate glove duties come from a different trade law: the U.S. trade office decided to “increase the rate of additional duties on medical gloves to 50 percent in 2025” [37].
  • Because After the restart, SafeSource announced in August that it was “suspending activity immediately at its nitrile glove and man-made fiber PPE plants because of poor market conditions” [38]. Its president said those conditions “do not permit sustained domestic production.” [38]
  • So Production did not last at that maker while the emergency taxes were in place. The Malaysian import tax and statements supporting U.S. factories do not establish an available medical backup that the bill would put at risk.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: The July article on SafeSource says the firm's imported nitrile chemicals became subject to the 10% base tariff. SafeSource suspended its U.S. glove and PPE plants on August 22, 2025, putting 541 employees out of work, and cited market conditions unsupportive for several years. Sources: [36], [38].

Evidence note: The researchers Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. The researchers Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases lost jobs compared with less exposed industries. A positive protection effect was offset by input costs (the cost of materials and parts) and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [39], [40].

arguments.title: The bill cuts costs that weaken military suppliers and military buying power.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill cuts costs that weaken military suppliers and military buying power.

  • Because Military supply chains use imported parts. Senator Shaheen identified sectors that “source a large part of their components from outside North America” [4].
  • Because The defense exemption from import taxes leaves out supplies shared between military and commercial work when tracking the two separately is too costly or impractical. The exemption’s exclusions cover supplies “identical in nature to supplies purchased by the Contractor or any subcontractor in connection with its commercial business” [5] when “It is not economical or feasible to account for such supplies so as to ensure that the amount of the supplies for which duty-free entry is claimed does not exceed the amount purchased in connection with this contract.” [5]
  • Because Costs that suppliers must pay themselves threaten the firms and workers that make military equipment. Shaheen warned in April that this “could drive more companies and jobs out of the defense industrial supply chain, stifling innovation.” [4]
  • Because When suppliers pass higher costs to the military, the same budget buys less. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “As a result, the Department of Defense simply cannot buy as much with its budget.” [6]
  • So Ending these taxes on supplies outside the defense exemption removes a cost from military production.
  • So Protecting suppliers and military buying power strengthens the state's ability to equip its forces and defend its citizens.
arguments.con_html: No specific response to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: An October 6, 2025 legal report says a Pentagon memorandum clarified that the Duty-Free Entry clause in the Defense Department’s purchasing rules (DFARS) applies to tariffs as well as duties. It also says contractors failing to use the clause could absorb those costs. The clause excludes some commercial supplies mixed together with military supplies. Sources: [7], [5].
