arguments.title: The bill removes a barrier to joint defense with allies and partners.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill removes a barrier to joint defense with allies and partners.

  • Because The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, identifies tariffs on Australia as a threat to trust between the two allies: they have “the potential to significantly erode trust in the U.S.-Australia alliance.” [8]
  • Because Trade friction also limits closer defense ties with New Zealand. CSIS reports that this friction is “shrinking the permission space for New Zealand leaders to align more closely with the United States on key policy issues, such as potentially joining AUKUS Pillar II.” [8] “Permission space” means how much the public will accept.
  • Because AUKUS is a U.S. defense partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom. The 2022 U.S. security strategy explains its purpose: “Our AUKUS security partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom promotes stability in the Indo-Pacific while deepening defense and technology integration.” [9]
  • Because The damage also blocks joint action on China's trade practices. The research group Brookings concludes: “This means a coalition focused on addressing the trade challenges with China cannot be built while the United States treats its allies as economic rivals.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes removes a source of distrust and political resistance to cooperation. That helps the United States work with partners on shared defense and economic threats.

arguments.title: The bill lowers the cost of keeping supply options outside China.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill lowers the cost of keeping supply options outside China.

  • Because U.S. firms have moved production beyond China to protect supplies. CSIS, a research group, describes an effort to “diversify manufacturing supply chains and protect from shocks that were made apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic and from export controls, sanctions, and other punitive economic measures targeting China.” [13]
  • Because The taxes under this emergency also apply to goods from these other production sites. The research group Brookings reports: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers the cost of importing covered goods from those other suppliers. Cheaper supply options make it easier to keep backups against disruptions and foreign pressure. This strengthens U.S. resilience, meaning its ability to withstand shocks.
arguments.con_html:
Response This Point treats production outside China as evidence of supply routes protected from Chinese pressure. This response concerns the electronics evidence below and does not deny that some other supply options exist.

  • Because Brookings' cost comparison concerns manufacturing locations: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10] That comparison does not establish whether those factories can supply goods during a Chinese disruption.
  • Because Rhodium Group's review of electronics finds that “these emerging production hubs still rely heavily on Chinese components” [14], while “a range of countries like Malaysia and Singapore are also emerging as specialized component producers” [14]. A factory outside China can still depend on parts from China.
  • Because Rhodium identifies the resulting risk: “It also gives the Chinese government leverage over the pace and extent of de-risking” [14]. In plain words, China can still influence efforts to reduce dependence on it.
  • So A cheaper place to assemble goods does not by itself establish protection against pressure on their Chinese parts.

paths.necessity_reason: The cost falls only if the taxes stop on new imports from those suppliers. The later step to protection from Chinese pressure stays local and is the step the response challenges.

arguments.title: The bill removes a source of uncertainty that holds back investment.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 The bill removes a source of uncertainty that holds back investment.

  • Because The emergency lets the President raise these taxes by changing the official list of import tax rates (the HTSUS). The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [23]
  • Because Uncertainty has its own cost. Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, explain that “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs, likely causes firms to delay investment, potentially slowing economic activity even without any actual tariff changes” [22].
  • Because Production capacity is needed for defense. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “the United States needs people, materials, and production capacity to field military forces.” [6]
  • So Ending the emergency ends the power to change rates under the emergency. Removing that source of uncertainty helps firms plan investments in the production capacity the country needs to remain strong and withstand shocks.
arguments.con_html:

arguments.title: The bill removes a source of shocks to U.S. financial markets.

  • Because Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, traced a specific disruption to news about these taxes: “On the morning of Monday, April 7th, a rumored tariff pause and its swift rebuttal within minutes triggered significant intraday volatility in US Treasury yields and precipitated a sharp decline in liquidity across US Treasury cash and futures markets.” [24] Treasury securities are U.S. government debt. arguments.title: The bill uses a legal safeguard against unchecked emergency rule.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 9 The bill uses a legal safeguard against unchecked emergency rule.

  • Because The emergency concerns a long-lasting trade pattern: “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [23].
  • Because The Brennan Center, a law and policy group, explains the limit on emergency rule: “Emergency powers are not meant to solve long-standing problems, no matter how serious those problems may be. Nor are they intended to give a president the ability to bypass Congress and act as an all-powerful policymaker.” [26]
  • Because Congress has a lawful way to end this use of power. An emergency ends when “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” [2].
  • Because Divided powers help protect the country. The 2017 U.S. security strategy describes “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] The strategy adds: “We protect American sovereignty by defending these institutions, traditions, and principles” [27].
  • So Enacting the resolution applies Congress's legal check to this emergency. Keeping executive power (the power of the President) under standing rules protects dependable self-government. This supports the secure and stable state [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response This Point's assumption that a long-running problem cannot support this emergency is a contested reading of the law. This response does not deny that the resolution applies Congress's check.

  • Because The emergency law permits action against “any unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States” [28]. Its text does not say that a threat must be sudden or unforeseen. The age of the trade problem alone does not establish failure of that legal test.
  • Because The 2017 strategy's statement about “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] supports those safeguards in general. It does not establish that continuing this declaration would defeat them or threaten national stability.
  • So A lawful power to end an emergency, together with a general defense of constitutional safeguards, does not establish the misuse this Point relies on or a security benefit from ending this one.

arguments.title: The bill removes an extra incentive to make batteries needed by the U.S. military.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes an extra incentive to make batteries needed by the U.S. military.

  • Because The taxes under this emergency cover battery packs. In a September 10 ruling on a lithium-ion pack from China, U.S. Customs applied an “additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 percent” [34]. “Ad valorem” means a tax set as a percentage of the value.
  • Because Battery tariffs offer a way to shift purchases toward U.S. suppliers. Congress's research service explains: “Such a policy might pivot demand toward domestic producers of batteries and battery parts rather than imported sources” [35].
  • Because These are defense supplies. The Defense Department says: “More and more of our platforms, vehicles, and future capabilities rely on lithium-ion batteries.” [36]
  • Because Building U.S. battery production addresses a current military supply risk. In July 2025, government auditors reported efforts “to reduce reliance on foreign sources that are located primarily in China.” [37]
  • So The bill removes an extra incentive to buy U.S.-made batteries and invest in their production. Keeping that incentive supports the supply base for current and future military equipment. That serves [NAME]'s goal of a state able to defend its citizens.
arguments.con_html:
Response This Point jumps from a possible price incentive for battery makers to more secure military supplies. This response does not deny that the tax gives U.S. battery makers some price advantage.

  • Because The congressional report identifies a gap between making finished batteries and making their parts: “Domestic investment in further upstream activities, such as battery cell component manufacturing and active material manufacturing, has not kept pace with investment in further downstream processes.” [35]
  • Because Growth in commercial batteries also needs a link to military needs. The Defense Innovation Unit explains: “Low-demand signal and complex specifications make it challenging for DoD to leverage current commercial battery technology.” [38] The military buys small amounts and needs batteries built to its requirements. DoD means the Defense Department.
  • So This Point has not shown that this extra tax adds U.S. capacity for the cells, materials or usable batteries needed to reduce military reliance on China. A price incentive alone does not establish that security gain.

In July 2025, Malaysia announced a Strategic Trade Permit rule for U.S.-origin high-performance AI chips. Sources: [39], [7], [40], [41].

It describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff (an added tariff above the normal rate). USTR says courts can review the tools for maintaining those tariffs and that those tools may change. USTR also says it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. arguments.title: The bill gives up bargaining power to cut financial support for armed threats.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill gives up bargaining power to cut financial support for armed threats.

  • Because Malaysia's trade agreement promises cooperation under its own laws on U.S. sanctions lists, with the aim of “restricting transactions of its nationals with individuals and entities” [40] on those lists. These restrictions limit financial and business ties.
  • Because Businesses abroad help hide oil sales that pay for weapons and armed groups. The U.S. Treasury describes “creating the illusion of non-sanctionable trade between separate entities.” [48] Non-sanctionable trade is trade not barred by sanctions (U.S. penalties).
  • Because The Treasury reports that oil allocated to Iran's armed forces is “underwriting the development of ballistic missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as financing regional terrorist groups.” [48]
  • So The bill removes an extra tool for getting foreign help closing these ways of moving money. Keeping that tool serves [NAME]'s concern that the United States protect itself against armed threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response This Point does not connect Malaysia's promise to the oil network it cites. This response concerns that example and does not deny that the promise could reach other transactions by Malaysian nationals.

  • Because The promise concerns “restricting transactions of its nationals with individuals and entities” [40] on U.S. lists. The promise's reach depends on transactions involving Malaysian nationals.
  • Because The Treasury locates the cited front companies elsewhere: “These companies are established and operate in China” [48]. It also identifies “Singapore-based Oriental Apple Company PTE Ltd” [48]. Naming those firms does not identify a Malaysian transaction that the promise would restrict.
  • Because The Treasury's reference to Malaysian oil concerns false paperwork: a facilitator “likely provided falsified documents concealing the vessel’s identity and certifying its Iranian oil cargo as Malaysian heavy crude oil.” [48] A false cargo label does not establish involvement by Malaysian nationals.
  • So The oil-network evidence establishes a threat. It does not show a Malaysian restriction on that network that keeping this tariff threat would make more likely.

arguments.title: The bill lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching states the inherited duty: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [10].
  • Because A doll maker describes a tool for that teaching: “When you squeeze its hand, the Talking Jesus Doll speaks 10 of Jesus' phrases from the Bible – including the Lord's Prayer and John 3:16.” [12]
  • Because CBS News documented the maker's exposure to the earlier, higher tariffs: “With sky-high tariffs in place, he had paused shipments from China, and had containers of goods waiting in limbo overseas.” [13]
  • So Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids. Helping parents carry out the religious duty of passing their faith to children directly serves [NAME]'s wish to preserve Christian beliefs across generations.
arguments.con_html:
Response A seller's claim that a doll teaches Bible verses does not establish that the doll helps [NAME] pass on an accepted Christian tradition.

  • Because The maker states its aim: “The objective of the doll is to make the love and lessons of Jesus tangible for young children.” [12]
  • Because The Southern Baptist teaching calls parents to teach “spiritual and moral values” [10]. It does not identify this product as a way to do so.
  • Because The fit between images of Jesus and inherited Christian teaching cannot be assumed. Defending the rule in the Westminster catechism (a traditional Protestant teaching text) against such images, James Norris writes, “since an image of God cannot be a medium for worship it ought never to be a tool for education in the faith.” [14]
  • So This Point supplies the maker's purpose, but no basis for placing this aid within the tradition [NAME] seeks to keep. Lower import costs for the doll do not supply that missing link between the product and following [NAME]'s religion.

paths.original_excerpt: Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids.
paths.necessity_reason: The cost is removed only if the tax stops on new imports. The later link to inherited teaching stays local and is the step the response challenges.

arguments.title: Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.

  • Because Tariffs make goods from other countries cost more, which helps U.S. makers compete: “by making foreign goods more expensive, tariffs make domestic products more competitive.” [25] American Giant is one maker that produces in the United States: NPR reports that it “sources and manufactures almost all its products in the U.S., from cotton to the final stitch.” [26]
  • Because A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.” [27]
  • Because Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27]
  • Because Marriage and the husband's role as provider are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” [28] Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [28]
  • Because That family pattern also carries a duty to pass on the faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [28].
  • So By removing a defense against job and pay losses caused by imports, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
arguments.con_html:
Response A price advantage for U.S. products does not establish that these taxes protect the men's jobs and pay on which the family argument depends.

  • Because The bill says the April 2 emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] The comparison is keeping or ending its import taxes as of October 30, 2025.
  • Because The family study ties marriage losses to men's earnings compared with women's: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27] The study looks at rising Chinese import competition during 1990–2014, not the effects of these taxes.
  • Because A study of local employment under the 2018–2019 taxes reports that “import tariffs do not appear to increase employment in manufacturing” [29]. That study directly tests the step from import protection to factory jobs, which the marriage study does not test.
  • Because A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–2019 taxes found that “a positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs.” [30]
  • Because For the 2025 taxes, the president of the textile trade group warned in October: “Reciprocal tariffs on these items hurt domestic textile producers and drives offshoring, undermining U.S. manufacturing jobs” [31]. Offshoring means moving production to other countries. She was discussing taxes on certain imported materials and machinery not available in the United States.
  • So American Giant's U.S. production and a price advantage do not establish that this extra tax layer preserves men's jobs or pay. Without that link, the historical import losses do not establish that ending these taxes puts marriage, husbands' provider roles or passing on the faith at greater risk.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: The researchers Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. The researchers Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases lost jobs compared with less exposed industries. A positive protection effect was offset by input costs (the cost of materials and parts) and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [29], [30].

paths.necessity_reason: The family risk needs ending these taxes to reduce men's factory jobs or pay.

arguments.title: Removing price protection for U.S. factory work also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 Removing price protection for U.S. factory work also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.

  • Because A study using U.S. church data for 1990–2010 found that import shocks from China “led to a reduction in the number of churches” [32]. The study also found the shocks “caused an increase in the number of religious adherents” [32]. Adherents are members.
  • Because Members' money supports church life. The Southern Baptist faith statement calls for regular giving: “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally” [28]. Losing income leaves less money for that duty.
  • Because Losing local work can pull younger generations away from their congregations. The account of the closing of the Ragsdale Church of Christ reports, “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33].
  • Because A congregation is a place where families keep particular customs alive. Ragsdale's final gathering was “an old-time singing — the kind they used to have every fourth Sunday.” [33]
  • Because Worship there was also a family practice across generations. Member Emily Smartt “remembers being there with her parents and late husband.” [33]
  • So Ending this price protection for U.S. makers puts the jobs and income that help keep local congregations going at risk. Keeping those congregations and their shared customs alive honors [NAME]'s religious heritage. This gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.
arguments.con_html:
Response The church evidence does not show that keeping these taxes protects local congregations or their inherited customs.

  • Because The cited church-study summary examines “trade shocks to manufacturing industries stemming from Chinese imports” [32], using U.S. church data for 1990–2010. Applying its finding to this bill requires a step it does not test: that ending this tax layer harms the jobs or income that support congregations.
  • Because Ragsdale's preacher reported that “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33]. That example shows one reason members leave. It supplies no link between those departures and the import taxes this bill ends.
  • So Neither source establishes that ending these taxes would cut church income or drive members away. The duty to give and the value of shared worship customs do not fill that gap. This Point has not shown that the bill threatens the congregations that carry those customs.

The summary of the study by Cesur and co-authors finds fewer churches and more adherents following Chinese import shocks in 1990-2010. Sources: [33], [32].

SJRes88_UNN_support_05.response:
Response Ending the U.S. emergency is not itself the Chinese tariff decision or Chinese buying decision needed to reduce demand for Brazilian soy. This response does not address this Point's point about ending this emergency's power to raise tariffs further.

  • Because The bill's action concerns “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257” [1]. It does not change Chinese law.

SJRes88_UNC_support_01.support:
Point 1 Removing this emergency’s import taxes helps poorer families afford basic needs and eases an unequal burden.

  • Because The taxes raise shoppers' costs. An October study of the reciprocal taxes on clothing from Bangladesh explains: “The more likely outcome is that U.S. importers, retailers, and consumers will shoulder much of the additional cost.” [4]
  • Because Poorer households spend more of their income buying goods and services. Yale explains that “lower-income households spend a larger fraction of their income than higher-income households do, on average” [5].
  • Because People already buying the cheapest necessities have little room to cut costs. Marketplace explains: “If you’re already buying your underwear from the most affordable brands, there’s nothing cheaper to switch to.” [6] Marketplace also describes the food risk: “Because healthier food tends to be more expensive, and if you can’t afford the cheapest vegetables, then you don’t buy any.” [6]
  • So Ending these taxes removes pressure on the price of necessities. This protects food and clothing budgets where money is tightest. Protecting those least able to pay serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment.

An April 2025 Marketplace article says prices of some goods may not fall back after tariffs are removed if demand stays high or firms rebuild supply chains. It says prices of goods like fruit and vegetables may be less sticky (less likely to stay high), and prices likely decline if demand had fallen. Sources: [7].
SJRes88_UNC_support_01.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_UNC_support_02.support:
Point 2 Easing import tax costs gives small business owners a fairer chance to keep their livelihoods and the jobs they support.

  • Because The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a business group, reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs” [8].
  • Because Small firms have fewer ways to handle tariff costs than larger rivals. CNBC explains: “Their margins are slimmer, their supply chains less diverse and their negotiating power with vendors dampened by the smaller sizes of their orders.” [9] Margins are the profit left after costs, and vendors are sellers.
  • Because These costs can take money away from jobs. At Reekon Tools, a small tool company, “The hundreds of thousands of dollars Reed planned to use to hire between three and five designers and engineers is now going to tariffs instead, he said.” [9]
  • So Ending the emergency's taxes frees money that affected firms need to operate and hire. It removes a burden that people running smaller firms are less able to absorb. That supports fair opportunities to earn a living for owners and workers.

CNBC reports Reekon's total expected 2025 tariffs at more than $400,000, without separating this emergency’s tariffs from other tariffs. Sources: [9].

SJRes88_UNC_support_03.support:
Point 3 Ending the emergency, a source of sudden import tax changes, protects access to jobs and safe work.

  • Because The April 2 order allows further tax rises, including power to “increase duties under this order” [10].
  • Because Uncertainty about tariff rates holds back staffing. In its June 2025 survey of firms in the Fourth Federal Reserve District (a region served by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland), the Cleveland Fed found that “19 percent of contacts said that tariff-related uncertainty had led their firm to scale back staffing plans” [11].
  • Because Uncertainty also threatens workers' protection abroad. Asked about tariff uncertainty, Sara Park of the International Labour Organization (ILO) explained: “During periods of crisis or uncertainty, investment generally pauses. One concern is that factories stop investing in improving working conditions, which could affect occupational safety and health.” [12]
  • So Ending the emergency removes its power to change these tax rates again. That removes a source of pressure to hold back hiring and safety improvements. Protecting opportunities to find paid work and stay safe at work serves [NAME]'s concern for workers, including vulnerable workers abroad.
SJRes88_UNC_support_03.response:
Response Closing one legal way of making sudden tax changes does not establish less uncertainty about the rates firms would actually pay. This response does not deny that the bill ends this order's own power to raise rates.

  • Because Replacement plans were announced before the vote. In a May interview transcribed in a June 2 court filing, trade adviser Peter Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [13] Here, “lose” means lose in court. This was a stated plan to keep the tariff policy after losing its emergency-law basis.
  • Because An October 2025 analysis described a possible temporary step toward other tariff powers: “Five months of Section 122 tariffs would provide time for the Commerce Department to do the investigation required by Section 232 of the Trade Act of 1962 for a president to impose tariffs for national security reasons.” [14] Using Section 122 would still have to meet the conditions in that law.
  • So Hiring and safety plans respond to uncertainty about future rates, whichever law sets them. Given the announced search for replacement powers, this Point's evidence does not establish that ending this legal way of setting tariffs would make rates more predictable.

SJRes88_UNC_support_04.support:

  • Because China directly answered the April taxes with taxes on U.S. exports. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, says that “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [15].
  • Because Retaliation puts sellers at a disadvantage: “Foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports make U.S. goods less competitive in foreign markets compared to goods not subject to tariffs” [15]. October reporting shows what this can mean for farm income: one Minnesota grower was selling soybeans “for less than what it cost to produce them.” [16]
  • Because Reducing the U.S. taxes has already helped ease this conflict. The May 2025 joint agreement paired U.S. tariff cuts with China's commitment to “suspend or remove the non-tariff countermeasures taken against the United States since April 2, 2025.” [17] Non-tariff countermeasures are responses other than taxes on goods.
  • So Ending these taxes and their power to fuel new rounds of retaliation reduces an avoidable risk to export sales. Protecting people whose livelihoods are caught in that conflict gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

China's March 2025 farm duties responded to a U.S. action separate from the April 2 emergency. On October 30, 2025, China said the U.S. would suspend the 24 percent reciprocal tariff for another year and that China would adjust its countermeasures, and reported consensus on expanding agricultural trade.   • Because The reciprocal taxes threaten demand for these workers' goods. The October clothing study warns that “the elevated tariffs are set to reduce demand, squeeze suppliers, and depress investment in future capacity” [4].
  • Because This reaches an important source of women's earnings. UN Trade and Development's October 30 report states: “The textile and apparel industry, an important source of employment for women in many LDCs, has been hit hardest.” [20] LDCs are countries the U.N. classifies as least developed.

  • So Removing the added tax supports demand for workers' goods and investment in future production. That protects earnings for food, schooling and healthcare, women's ability to earn, and poorer countries' paths to better work. These are reasons for [NAME], who values protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.

  • Because The emergency's stated problem is reflected in “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [10]. A trade deficit means the United States buys more goods from abroad than it sells abroad.
  • Because Small, poor economies have little ability to buy U.S. goods. The U.N. explains: “As many of these economies are small in size, structurally weak with low purchasing power, they offer limited export market opportunities for the US.” [22]
  • Because Lesotho shows the mismatch. Its share of the U.S. goods trade deficit in the U.N.'s 2024 data was tiny: “Lesotho 0.019%” [23]. Lesotho still faced an added tax under the later rates. September 2025 reporting describes “a much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21].
  • So Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people whose countries have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Fair treatment calls for burdens to reflect people's circumstances and their part in the problem. Sparing poor people this disproportionate burden serves [NAME]'s concern for justice across borders.
SJRes88_UNC_support_06.response:
Response The deficit-share comparison does not establish the unfair treatment it is used to prove.

  • Because The U.N.'s “Lesotho 0.019%” [23] measures a country’s share of the total U.S. goods trade deficit. The reported “much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21] measures a tax on the value of covered imports. Neither percentage measures the tax cost compared with a poor person’s income.
  • Because This Point adds a rule that the burden is unjust because the country contributes little to the total deficit. [NAME]’s concern for just treatment of people does not by itself establish that national trade shares determine the burdens individuals should bear.
  • So A small country’s small share of a large country’s deficit is not a measure of injustice to its workers. The two percentages do not support the claimed disproportionate burden or show that ending it would correct unjust treatment.

SJRes88_UNC_support_07.support:

The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, explains that it “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [24]
  • Because Careful review helps protect people who bear the costs. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce calls for “appropriate stakeholder consultation and a methodical assessment of costs” [8] before raising taxes on traded goods.
  • Because This bill makes Congress's power to end that use of emergency authority effective. CRS explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [24]
  • So People whose food budgets and jobs are at stake deserve public review of burdens placed on them. Ending this emergency enforces Congress's check on a way of taxing that does not require an investigation. That supports [NAME]'s concern that everyone be treated justly.

Executive Order 14257 says the President received final results of investigations ordered by earlier memoranda on April 1, 2025. CRS says IEEPA does not require any agency to investigate or make findings. SJRes88_SEP_support_02.support:

SJRes88_SEP_support_02.response:
Response Lower hospital supply costs do not establish the lower patient charges on which this care-access argument depends. This response does not settle what happens when contracts and premiums are reset.

  • Because The sentence about higher patient charges follows a conditional step: “In the near term, financial pressures could incentivize hospitals to seek higher reimbursement rates from insurers.” [6]
  • Because The hospital association’s October 17 letter explains who bears costs under existing payment rules: “Given that hospital payments are set by government and private payer contracts, the costs would be borne by hospitals directly.” [7]
  • So A tax saving does not itself change an agreed payment rate. This Point does not establish how savings would reach patients through lower bills, premiums or deductibles and improve access to care.

SJRes88_SEP_support_03.support:
Point 3 Lower supply costs help hospitals and ambulance services keep staff, services, and reliable equipment.

  • Because Supply costs compete with care budgets: “Rising supply costs force budget reallocation, limiting investment in staff, technology, and patient care.” [8]
  • Because The hospital association cites a survey, taken in January 2025 before the April emergency, in which administrators expected to “delay equipment upgrades to manage financial strain.” [5]
  • Because Equipment quality matters for finding illness. One surveyed administrator explains: “We do not want to misdiagnose a patient because we have decided to use lower quality equipment that cannot detect their issue.” [8]
  • Because Ambulance services also depend on imports. In April 2025, their association warned about imported supplies and medicines. Medicines were exempt from these taxes. The association wrote: “Tariffs on any of these items will increase prices, and could result in product shortages, additional supply chain complexity, and other challenges that EMS simply cannot afford.” [9] EMS means emergency medical services.
  • So Removing taxes on covered supplies eases pressure to cut staff, services or equipment spending. That protects [NAME]’s access to emergency help and accurate diagnosis.

The health news outlet Becker's reports on a survey by the research firm Black Book, cited in the American Hospital Association (AHA) statement. It reports that the survey was conducted in late January 2025, before the April emergency, and that it covered tariffs on Chinese imports, including expected medicine costs. Sources: [10].
SJRes88_SEP_support_03.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

strength.html: The letter from the National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians (NAEMT) dates from April 2025. It cites persistent low payment for emergency medical services (EMS) and asks the Administration to consider EMS impacts of additional tariff actions. Sources: [9].

SJRes88_SEP_support_04.support:
Point 4 Ending this emergency’s import taxes protects research on better ways to prevent and treat disease.

  • Because Disease research needs imports that a Johns Hopkins report described in April 2025 as taxed: “Biomedical labs rely heavily on imported equipment and materials, from microscopes to diagnostic tools, much of which is now subject to steep tariffs.” [11]
  • Because Higher supply costs threaten that work, according to an expert named Dai in the same report: “Without affordable access to essential supplies, he warns, American biomedical research could slow down” [11].
  • Because Medical device makers also face pressure on research and development, meaning work on new or better products: “U.S. companies have been shifting resources to manage tariff costs, with R&D spending expected to be the most heavily impacted.” [3]
  • Because That research serves patients. The industry describes its focus as “patient-centered diagnostics and treatments” [3], meaning ways to find and treat illness.
  • So Removing these costs protects the research that better tests and treatments depend on. This advances [NAME]’s goal of avoiding and overcoming disease.

One line of the official U.S. import tax list (HTSUS 9810.00.60) gives duty-free treatment (no import tax) to approved scientific instruments for nonprofit educational or scientific institutions. August 2025 customs guidance excludes entries under Chapter 98 of that list from the additional duties, with exceptions. Sources: [12], [13].
SJRes88_SEP_support_04.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_05.support:
Point 5 Lower food costs help protect a diet that prevents disease.

  • Because Nutritious imports remained taxed in late October. An October 24 report confirmed that major banana suppliers remained covered by the tax. An economist explained that “we absolutely should expect a 10% tax on banana imports to drive banana prices higher” [14].
  • Because Higher prices can worsen diets: “During periods of rising prices or uncertainty, households often shift from perishable nutritious foods towards cheaper, longer lasting processed items, reducing the overall quality of the diet.” [15]
  • Because The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the U.S. public health agency, explains why fruits and vegetables matter: “they contribute important nutrients, can reduce the risk for many chronic diseases, and can also help with weight management.” [16]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers a barrier to nutritious food. This helps [NAME] protect their health.
SJRes88_SEP_support_05.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

strength.html: CNBC reports bananas up 5.4% since April, without measuring consumption. A commentary in the medical journal BMJ says tariffs may raise both healthy and unhealthy food costs and fall most on lower-income households. Sources: [14], [15].

SJRes88_SEP_support_06.support:
Point 6 Reducing pressure for layoffs protects workers’ health.

  • Because Businesses absorbing higher import costs face options including “reduce headcount to offset costs or close shop and go out of business.” [17] To reduce headcount means to employ fewer people.
  • Because Job threats affect health: “uncertainty and feelings of job insecurity can harm workers’ mental health, performance, and productivity at work.” [18]
  • So Ending these added costs reduces pressure on employers to cut jobs and the related threat to health. This is an ordinary risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.
SJRes88_SEP_support_06.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_07.support:
Point 7 Lower costs for everyday goods leave more money for medicine and care.

  • Because Higher import costs reach household budgets: “Most of these costs are likely to be passed along to American consumers.” [17]
  • Because A survey conducted in October found that some respondents “delayed or skipped buying doctor-prescribed medication in the past year due to their finances” [19].
  • So Removing these added charges leaves more income available for medicine and medical visits. This helps [NAME] keep up needed treatment.
SJRes88_SEP_support_07.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_08.support:
Point 8 Ending a source of financial stress from higher prices protects health.

  • Because A May 2025 survey of reactions to tariffs found “most participants reporting emotions like stress, pessimism, frustration, or anxiety.” [20]
  • Because Stress affects health, beyond unpleasant feelings. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the U.S. public health agency, lists “Nightmares or problems sleeping” [21] and “Physical reactions, such as headaches, body pains, stomach problems, or skin rashes” [21].
  • So Ending this source of higher prices removes a cause of financial worry and its health risks. This serves [NAME]’s concern for health.

The result from the research firm Reach3 is a press release on consumer feelings, and it combines negative emotions into one category. CDC lists possible effects of stress in general. Sources: [20], [21].
SJRes88_SEP_support_08.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_09.support:
Point 9 More affordable alarms and fire alerts help protect homes.

  • Because The Security Industry Association, a trade group, warned in April that global tariffs “will directly increase the cost of essential security and life safety products” [22].
  • Because These products protect households: “Consumers need access to alarm and camera systems and fire prevention and alert devices to keep their homes safe.” [22]
  • So Removing taxes on covered safety products lowers a barrier to protection against break-ins and fire. This helps [NAME] stay personally safe.
SJRes88_SEP_support_09.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_10.support:
Point 10 Lower costs for water treatment help protect safe drinking water.

  • Because Reporting on the April 2 tariffs explains the risk to imported treatment equipment: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” [23] Water utilities are the organizations that supply water.
  • Because Treatment protects health: “Drinking water utilities clean (treat) water to remove harmful germs and chemicals and meet safety standards.” [24]
  • So Removing taxes on covered equipment helps utilities pay for the treatment and maintenance that protect [NAME] from contaminated drinking water.

In August 2025, 407 product codes were added to the metal tariffs under Section 232, a separate trade law. For those goods, the metal content falls under Section 232 and the rest remains subject to reciprocal tariffs. Sources: [25], [26].
SJRes88_SEP_support_10.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_11.support:
Point 11 More affordable helmets help prevent cycling injuries.

  • Because In May 2025, when much higher rates applied to goods from China, the cycling group PeopleForBikes warned that current and proposed helmet tariffs make protection “much less affordable, which could leave both adults and children unprotected from potential injury.” [27]
  • So Removing these added taxes lowers a barrier to wearing protection during an ordinary activity. This serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury.

The helmet letter was reported in May 2025, when China faced tariffs of 145%. By the bill date the higher rate was suspended, a 10% reciprocal rate remained, and other U.S. tariffs on China remained. Sources: [27], [28].
SJRes88_SEP_support_11.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_support_12.support:
Point 12 Lower costs for workplace safety gear help prevent injuries.

  • Because A safety equipment industry report on tariffs enacted on and after April 2 warns about personal protective equipment, or PPE: “the current tariffs will drive up PPE costs across the board, leaving companies with few options: raise prices, cut labor, or reduce their investment in safety equipment.” [29]
  • Because Cutting protection threatens personal safety. The report warns of “preventable injuries and fatalities” [29].
  • So Ending these taxes removes pressure to cut workplace protection. This reduces an injury risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.

The study by the International Safety Equipment Association (ISEA) covers tariffs enacted on and after April 2, 2025. An Inc. report on the study describes purchasing cuts without separating tariffs by the law behind them. Sources: [29], [30].
SJRes88_SEP_support_12.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SEP_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 The bill removes support for U.S. medical-supply factories that provide a backup during health emergencies.

  • Because The taxes under this emergency cover medical gloves from suppliers beyond China. For rubber surgical gloves, an October 9 analysis records a “19% tariff on those from Malaysia” [32]. The October 26 Malaysia agreement keeps “at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025” [33].
  • Because U.S. medical-supply makers explain the link to emergency production: “Reciprocal tariffs aren’t just about fairness; they’re about ensuring that our nation can produce life-saving medical supplies when they matter most.” [34]
  • Because Reliable supplies protect patients and the public. The U.S. health department says protective gear and medical equipment “serve vital roles in protecting patients, healthcare workers, and the public.” [35] It also identifies the need to keep U.S. suppliers in business: “the U.S. Government has a vested interest in U.S. companies' continued marketplace viability” [35].
  • So Ending the tax removes a price advantage for U.S.-made gloves and removes support for keeping that production available when overseas supplies are disrupted.
  • So [NAME] needs protection from infection and safe medical care. Keeping that backup supply gives [NAME] a personal health reason to oppose the bill.
SJRes88_SEP_oppose_01.response:
Response This Point's price advantage does not establish that these emergency taxes keep medical backup production available. This response does not deny that the tax gives U.S.-made gloves some price advantage over Malaysian gloves.

  • Because A U.S. glove maker's restart was linked to taxes on China: “new U.S. tariffs on rubber gloves from China have doubled the price from a few months ago” [36]; “SafeSource restarted two production lines to accommodate recent new orders” [36].
  • Because The bill targets “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025” [1]. China’s separate glove duties come from a different trade law: the U.S. trade office decided to “increase the rate of additional duties on medical gloves to 50 percent in 2025” [37].
  • Because After the restart, SafeSource announced in August that it was “suspending activity immediately at its nitrile glove and man-made fiber PPE plants because of poor market conditions” [38]. Its president said those conditions “do not permit sustained domestic production.” [38]
  • So Production did not last at that maker while the emergency taxes were in place. The Malaysian import tax and statements supporting U.S. factories do not establish an available medical backup that the bill would put at risk.

The July article on SafeSource says the firm's imported nitrile chemicals became subject to the 10% base tariff. SafeSource suspended its U.S. glove and PPE plants on August 22, 2025, putting 541 employees out of work, and cited market conditions unsupportive for several years. Sources: [36], [38].

The researchers Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. The researchers Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases lost jobs compared with less exposed industries. A positive protection effect was offset by input costs (the cost of materials and parts) and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [39], [40].

SJRes88_SES_support_01.support:
Point 1 The bill cuts costs that weaken military suppliers and military buying power.

  • Because Military supply chains use imported parts. Senator Shaheen identified sectors that “source a large part of their components from outside North America” [4].
  • Because The defense exemption from import taxes leaves out supplies shared between military and commercial work when tracking the two separately is too costly or impractical. The exemption’s exclusions cover supplies “identical in nature to supplies purchased by the Contractor or any subcontractor in connection with its commercial business” [5] when “It is not economical or feasible to account for such supplies so as to ensure that the amount of the supplies for which duty-free entry is claimed does not exceed the amount purchased in connection with this contract.” [5]
  • Because Costs that suppliers must pay themselves threaten the firms and workers that make military equipment. Shaheen warned in April that this “could drive more companies and jobs out of the defense industrial supply chain, stifling innovation.” [4]
  • Because When suppliers pass higher costs to the military, the same budget buys less. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “As a result, the Department of Defense simply cannot buy as much with its budget.” [6]
  • So Ending these taxes on supplies outside the defense exemption removes a cost from military production.
  • So Protecting suppliers and military buying power strengthens the state's ability to equip its forces and defend its citizens.

An October 6, 2025 legal report says a Pentagon memorandum clarified that the Duty-Free Entry clause in the Defense Department’s purchasing rules (DFARS) applies to tariffs as well as duties. It also says contractors failing to use the clause could absorb those costs. The clause excludes some commercial supplies mixed together with military supplies. Sources: [7], [5].
SJRes88_SES_support_01.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SES_support_02.support:
Point 2 The bill removes a barrier to joint defense with allies and partners.

  • Because The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, identifies tariffs on Australia as a threat to trust between the two allies: they have “the potential to significantly erode trust in the U.S.-Australia alliance.” [8]
  • Because Trade friction also limits closer defense ties with New Zealand. CSIS reports that this friction is “shrinking the permission space for New Zealand leaders to align more closely with the United States on key policy issues, such as potentially joining AUKUS Pillar II.” [8] “Permission space” means how much the public will accept.
  • Because AUKUS is a U.S. defense partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom. The 2022 U.S. security strategy explains its purpose: “Our AUKUS security partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom promotes stability in the Indo-Pacific while deepening defense and technology integration.” [9]
  • Because The damage also blocks joint action on China's trade practices. The research group Brookings concludes: “This means a coalition focused on addressing the trade challenges with China cannot be built while the United States treats its allies as economic rivals.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes removes a source of distrust and political resistance to cooperation. That helps the United States work with partners on shared defense and economic threats.
SJRes88_SES_support_02.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

strength.html: Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].
CSIS reports public support for the U.S.-Australia alliance remains high despite tariffs, and recommends greater consistency in U.S. policy. Sources: [8].

SJRes88_SES_support_03.support:
Point 3 The bill lowers the cost of keeping supply options outside China.

  • Because U.S. firms have moved production beyond China to protect supplies. CSIS, a research group, describes an effort to “diversify manufacturing supply chains and protect from shocks that were made apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic and from export controls, sanctions, and other punitive economic measures targeting China.” [13]
  • Because The taxes under this emergency also apply to goods from these other production sites. The research group Brookings reports: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers the cost of importing covered goods from those other suppliers. Cheaper supply options make it easier to keep backups against disruptions and foreign pressure. This strengthens U.S. resilience, meaning its ability to withstand shocks.
SJRes88_SES_support_03.response:
Response This Point treats production outside China as evidence of supply routes protected from Chinese pressure. This response concerns the electronics evidence below and does not deny that some other supply options exist.

  • Because Brookings' cost comparison concerns manufacturing locations: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10] That comparison does not establish whether those factories can supply goods during a Chinese disruption.
  • Because Rhodium Group's review of electronics finds that “these emerging production hubs still rely heavily on Chinese components” [14], while “a range of countries like Malaysia and Singapore are also emerging as specialized component producers” [14]. A factory outside China can still depend on parts from China.
  • Because Rhodium identifies the resulting risk: “It also gives the Chinese government leverage over the pace and extent of de-risking” [14]. In plain words, China can still influence efforts to reduce dependence on it.
  • So A cheaper place to assemble goods does not by itself establish protection against pressure on their Chinese parts.

SJRes88_SES_support_04.support:
Point 4 The bill reduces pressure on essential water systems.

  • Because Water utilities (the organizations that supply water) rely on foreign equipment: “U.S. water systems are deeply reliant on imported gear” [15].
  • Because Higher import costs squeeze utility budgets. WaterWorld's analysis of the April 2 order states: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities. These increased costs could translate into higher utility rates and budget constraints.” [16]
  • Because Those costs threaten maintenance: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” [16]
  • Because Water services protect the public from disease. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) states: “Safe drinking water is a prerequisite for protecting public health and all human activity, and properly treated wastewater is vital for preventing disease and protecting the environment.” [17]
  • Because Emergency response also depends on water. The same EPA plan lists “Firefighting and hazardous material spill and event responses” [17] among emergency services that need drinking water supplies.
  • So Ending these taxes on covered treatment equipment removes a cost obstacle to timely repairs and upgrades.
  • So Keeping water and sewage systems working protects the public from disease and supports emergency response. This strengthens the country's ability to protect its citizens.

Water Daily's April 2025 article says "No federal carve-outs so far," meaning no federal exceptions, while Customs guidance excludes some Canadian and Mexican goods. An October water-equipment warning concerns Section 232 metals duties, which the bill leaves in place. Sources: [15], [3], [18].
SJRes88_SES_support_04.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SES_support_05.support:
Point 5 The bill protects medical supplies needed for surgery and infection control.

  • Because Hospitals depend on foreign supplies: “international sources supply a significant proportion of essential medical goods.” [19]
  • Because These include devices that prevent infection: “Some of these devices are single-use, designed to protect patients from infection, such as single-use blood pressure cuffs, stethoscope covers and sterile drapes.” [19]
  • Because The American Hospital Association warns that tariffs “may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” [19] Vendors are sellers.
  • Because Supply disruptions “would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” [19].
  • Because Higher costs also threaten the continued provision of care: “Persistent expense growth threatens hospitals’ solvency and ability to sustain comprehensive services in their communities.” [19] Solvency means having enough money to keep operating.
  • So Ending these taxes on covered medical devices removes a cost and supply risk from hospitals. Ending the taxes helps preserve the country's ability to protect people from serious illness and infection.

The health news outlet Becker's reports on a survey by the research firm Black Book, cited in the American Hospital Association (AHA) statement. It reports that the survey was conducted in late January 2025, before the April emergency, and that it covered tariffs on Chinese imports, including expected medicine costs. Sources: [20].
SJRes88_SES_support_05.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_SES_support_06.support:
Point 6 The bill eases economic strain across the country.

  • Because The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a business group, reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs, with additional economic pain likely in the coming months.” [21]
  • Because Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, explain that “rising global tariffs dampen economic growth by disrupting trade flows, misallocating resources, and increasing input costs for businesses and goods prices for consumers” [22].
  • Because Economic strength supports national security and social cohesion, meaning people holding together as a society. The 2022 U.S. security strategy calls the middle class “critical to our national security as an engine of economic growth and a key source of democratic vibrance and cohesion.” [9]
  • So Removing these taxes eases costs and trade disruption for U.S. firms and households. Reducing that nationwide strain supports the economic base of a strong, stable country.
SJRes88_SES_support_06.response:
Response This Point moves from evidence about prices and growth to a claim about national protection and social stability without establishing that step.

  • Because The Chamber reports that businesses “are struggling with higher costs” [21]. Federal Reserve researchers describe how tariffs “dampen economic growth by disrupting trade flows, misallocating resources, and increasing input costs for businesses and goods prices for consumers” [22]. These statements concern costs and economic activity.
  • Because The security strategy calls the middle class “critical to our national security as an engine of economic growth and a key source of democratic vibrance and cohesion.” [9] The strategy does not establish that the particular costs removed here threaten that cohesion or the country's ability to protect its citizens.
  • So An economic gain and a reduction in threats to national stability are different outcomes. This Point's general statement about the middle class does not establish the security effect of this particular tax change.

SJRes88_SES_support_07.support:
Point 7 The bill removes a source of uncertainty that holds back investment.

  • Because The emergency lets the President raise these taxes by changing the official list of import tax rates (the HTSUS). The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [23]
  • Because Uncertainty has its own cost. Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, explain that “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs, likely causes firms to delay investment, potentially slowing economic activity even without any actual tariff changes” [22].
  • Because Production capacity is needed for defense. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “the United States needs people, materials, and production capacity to field military forces.” [6]
  • So Ending the emergency ends the power to change rates under the emergency. Removing that source of uncertainty helps firms plan investments in the production capacity the country needs to remain strong and withstand shocks.
SJRes88_SES_support_07.response:
Response This Point equates ending rate changes under one order with reducing the policy uncertainty that delays investment. This response does not deny that this order's own power to change rates would end.

  • Because The bill ends the emergency “declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257” [1]. The bill's text does not end other tariff powers.
  • Because Commerce Secretary Lutnick had announced replacement action if the emergency tariff power were blocked: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [11] In September 2025, Treasury Secretary Bessent again said, “And there are lots of other authorities that can be used - not as efficient, not as powerful,” [12]. The stated plan to replace blocked tariffs gives firms a concrete policy to consider.
  • Because The Federal Reserve's finding concerns firms' response to “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs” [22]. Firms planning investment must consider the announced plan for replacement as well as what happens to this one order.
  • So Repeal would leave firms facing decisions about replacement tariffs and their rates. This Point has not shown that ending this legal way of setting tariffs would ease the uncertainty holding back the production investment it relies on.

Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].

SJRes88_SES_support_08.support:
Point 8 The bill removes a source of shocks to U.S. financial markets.

  • Because Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, traced a specific disruption to news about these taxes: “On the morning of Monday, April 7th, a rumored tariff pause and its swift rebuttal within minutes triggered significant intraday volatility in US Treasury yields and precipitated a sharp decline in liquidity across US Treasury cash and futures markets.” [24] Treasury securities are U.S. government debt. In plain words, a rumor about a tariff pause and its quick denial made the interest rates on this debt swing during one day, and made this debt harder to trade.
  • Because Liquidity means how easily an asset can be bought and sold. The Federal Reserve explains the danger: “In extreme cases, low liquidity can threaten continued market functioning, leading to a situation in which participants are unable to trade without incurring a significant cost.” [25]
  • Because This concerns a core part of U.S. finance: “Treasury market liquidity is particularly important because of the key role these securities play in the financial system.” [25]
  • So Ending this tariff program removes a source of sudden policy news that has strained trading in U.S. government debt. Reducing that risk supports the country's financial stability.
SJRes88_SES_support_08.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

strength.html: Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].
The Federal Reserve note compares April 2025 Treasury market stress with "much-improved market conditions in September 2025." It does not estimate the effect of ending this emergency. Sources: [24].

Officials said the policy would continue another way. Trade adviser Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [UNC 13] Commerce Secretary Lutnick said: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [SES 11] An October 2025 analysis says other laws “could result in similar ends” [UNC 14]. So firms and markets could still face uncertainty about rates under other laws.

SJRes88_SES_support_09.support:
Point 9 The bill uses a legal safeguard against unchecked emergency rule.

  • Because The emergency concerns a long-lasting trade pattern: “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [23].
  • Because The Brennan Center, a law and policy group, explains the limit on emergency rule: “Emergency powers are not meant to solve long-standing problems, no matter how serious those problems may be. Nor are they intended to give a president the ability to bypass Congress and act as an all-powerful policymaker.” [26]
  • Because Congress has a lawful way to end this use of power. An emergency ends when “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” [2].
  • Because Divided powers help protect the country. The 2017 U.S. security strategy describes “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] The strategy adds: “We protect American sovereignty by defending these institutions, traditions, and principles” [27].
  • So Enacting the resolution applies Congress's legal check to this emergency. Keeping executive power (the power of the President) under standing rules protects dependable self-government. This supports the secure and stable state [NAME] values.

A November 2025 letter from senators says multiple courts found these tariffs go beyond what IEEPA (the emergency powers law) allows, and an October analysis says the Court of International Trade and Federal Circuit ruled against them; the Supreme Court had the case on the bill date. Sources: [29], [30], [28].
SJRes88_SES_support_09.response:
Response This Point's assumption that a long-running problem cannot support this emergency is a contested reading of the law. This response does not deny that the resolution applies Congress's check.

  • Because The emergency law permits action against “any unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States” [28]. Its text does not say that a threat must be sudden or unforeseen. The age of the trade problem alone does not establish failure of that legal test.
  • Because The 2017 strategy's statement about “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] supports those safeguards in general. It does not establish that continuing this declaration would defeat them or threaten national stability.
  • So A lawful power to end an emergency, together with a general defense of constitutional safeguards, does not establish the misuse this Point relies on or a security benefit from ending this one.

The standard in the law is "unusual and extraordinary threat." Sources: [29], [30], [28].

SJRes88_SES_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 The bill removes an extra incentive to make batteries needed by the U.S. military.

  • Because The taxes under this emergency cover battery packs. In a September 10 ruling on a lithium-ion pack from China, U.S. Customs applied an “additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 percent” [34]. “Ad valorem” means a tax set as a percentage of the value.
  • Because Battery tariffs offer a way to shift purchases toward U.S. suppliers. Congress's research service explains: “Such a policy might pivot demand toward domestic producers of batteries and battery parts rather than imported sources” [35].
  • Because These are defense supplies. The Defense Department says: “More and more of our platforms, vehicles, and future capabilities rely on lithium-ion batteries.” [36]
  • Because Building U.S. battery production addresses a current military supply risk. In July 2025, government auditors reported efforts “to reduce reliance on foreign sources that are located primarily in China.” [37]
  • So The bill removes an extra incentive to buy U.S.-made batteries and invest in their production. Keeping that incentive supports the supply base for current and future military equipment. That serves [NAME]'s goal of a state able to defend its citizens.

The U.S. toolmaker Jergens gains partly from tariff-avoiding orders and partly from defense demand. The duty-free clause in the Defense Department’s purchasing rules (DFARS) covers goods for final Defense Department (DoD) products. The Malaysia agreement can be terminated on 180 days' notice. In July 2025, Malaysia announced a Strategic Trade Permit rule for U.S.-origin high-performance AI chips. Sources: [39], [7], [40], [41].
SJRes88_SES_oppose_01.response:
Response This Point jumps from a possible price incentive for battery makers to more secure military supplies. This response does not deny that the tax gives U.S. battery makers some price advantage.

The Defense Innovation Unit explains: “Low-demand signal and complex specifications make it challenging for DoD to leverage current commercial battery technology.” [38] The military buys small amounts and needs batteries built to its requirements. DoD means the Defense Department.
  • So This Point has not shown that this extra tax adds U.S. capacity for the cells, materials or usable batteries needed to reduce military reliance on China. A price incentive alone does not establish that security gain.

SJRes88_SES_oppose_02.support:

  • Because In the trade agreement signed October 26, Malaysia promises to work through its own rules to “align with all unilateral export controls in force by the United States, and ensure that its companies do not backfill or undermine these controls.” [40] These are rules limiting where sensitive goods can be sent. SJRes88_SES_oppose_04.response:
Response This Point does not connect Malaysia's promise to the oil network it cites. This response concerns that example and does not deny that the promise could reach other transactions by Malaysian nationals.

  • Because The promise concerns “restricting transactions of its nationals with individuals and entities” [40] on U.S. lists. The promise's reach depends on transactions involving Malaysian nationals.
  • Because The Treasury locates the cited front companies elsewhere: “These companies are established and operate in China” [48]. It also identifies “Singapore-based Oriental Apple Company PTE Ltd” [48]. Naming those firms does not identify a Malaysian transaction that the promise would restrict.
  • Because The Treasury's reference to Malaysian oil concerns false paperwork: a facilitator “likely provided falsified documents concealing the vessel’s identity and certifying its Iranian oil cargo as Malaysian heavy crude oil.” [48] A false cargo label does not establish involvement by Malaysian nationals.
  • So The oil-network evidence establishes a threat. It does not show a Malaysian restriction on that network that keeping this tariff threat would make more likely.

The U.S. Treasury says transactions with the firms it designated carry a risk of secondary sanctions (penalties on others who deal with them) under Executive Order 13224. Sources: [48], [49].
