SJRes88_TR_support_01.support:
Point 1 The bill helps churches keep familiar forms of worship music.

  • Because Tariffs raise the cost of imported instruments: “Now, tariffs are causing a big jump in costs for music stores.” [4]
  • Because Evangelical pastor Kevin DeYoung urges churches to keep an established practice: “But if your church already has an organ my advice is to keep using it.” [5]
  • Because DeYoung explains the purpose of the organ: “The organ fills in the cracks, provides an underneath sound, and encourages churches to sing louder and freer.” [5]
  • So When churches buy or replace covered imported instruments, the bill removes an added cost of keeping their familiar worship music. Preserving that religious practice serves [NAME]'s value of tradition.

The NPR price report says a large portion of musical instruments come from overseas. The stores it profiles sell or rent band instruments, one of them brass only, and it does not mention organs or churches. DeYoung's 2011 advice concerns a church that already has an organ. Executive Order 14257 covers all imported goods except listed exceptions. The annex tables that list them are not among the sources reviewed. Sources: [4], [5], [6].

The price report concerns stores selling or renting band instruments and does not mention organs or churches; the annex listing covered goods is not among the sources reviewed. This point's claim is limited to 'covered imported instruments'.
SJRes88_TR_support_01.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_TR_support_02.support:
Point 2 The bill helps families keep Christian Christmas customs.

  • Because A Christmas-tree importer reported higher prices caused by tariffs: “it also had to raise prices by 10% as a result of the tariffs.” [7]
  • Because The Christian group Focus on the Family describes a recurring custom that uses a Christmas tree: “A family slumber party by the Christmas tree is a tradition our kids love year after year.” [8]
  • Because Focus on the Family connects family celebrations to faith: “When we slow down to celebrate, we are showing our family that our faith matters—and that they matter.” [8]
  • So Removing the added tax on covered Christmas goods cuts a continuing cost of buying or replacing what these customs use. This helps [NAME] preserve family ways of celebrating Christian faith.
SJRes88_TR_support_02.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_TR_support_04.support:
Point 4 The bill lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching states the inherited duty: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [10].
  • Because A doll maker describes a tool for that teaching: “When you squeeze its hand, the Talking Jesus Doll speaks 10 of Jesus' phrases from the Bible – including the Lord's Prayer and John 3:16.” [12]
  • Because CBS News documented the maker's exposure to the earlier, higher tariffs: “With sky-high tariffs in place, he had paused shipments from China, and had containers of goods waiting in limbo overseas.” [13]
  • So Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids. Helping parents carry out the religious duty of passing their faith to children directly serves [NAME]'s wish to preserve Christian beliefs across generations.
SJRes88_TR_support_04.response:
Response A seller's claim that a doll teaches Bible verses does not establish that the doll helps [NAME] pass on an accepted Christian tradition.

  • Because The maker states its aim: “The objective of the doll is to make the love and lessons of Jesus tangible for young children.” [12]
  • Because The Southern Baptist teaching calls parents to teach “spiritual and moral values” [10]. It does not identify this product as a way to do so.
  • Because The fit between images of Jesus and inherited Christian teaching cannot be assumed. Defending the rule in the Westminster catechism (a traditional Protestant teaching text) against such images, James Norris writes, “since an image of God cannot be a medium for worship it ought never to be a tool for education in the faith.” [14]
  • So This Point supplies the maker's purpose, but no basis for placing this aid within the tradition [NAME] seeks to keep. Lower import costs for the doll do not supply that missing link between the product and following [NAME]'s religion.

SJRes88_TR_support_05.support:
Point 5 The bill helps families continue regular church offerings and Christmas gospel outreach.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching says “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [10]
  • Because An April 2025 report warned that price rises caused by tariffs put giving at risk: “At the same time, donors may give less as they face rising prices and a turbulent stock market.” [15]
  • So Reducing this pressure on household budgets helps protect families' ability to keep giving regular offerings and paying for church work.
  • Because Gift-based outreach is another established practice: “Operation Christmas Child has been collecting and delivering shoebox gifts to children worldwide for more than three decades.” [16]
  • Because Participants pack a “shoebox gift filled with fun toys, school supplies, and personal care items” [16]. These goods include a heavily imported product: “Over 80% of toys sold in the U.S. are made in China, according to The Toy Association trade group.” [13]
  • Because Evangelist Franklin Graham states the religious purpose: “these simple gifts open the door for the Gospel.” [16]
  • So Removing the added tax on commercially imported toys bought for these gifts lowers a cost of continuing this outreach. Regular church offerings and this established Christmas gospel practice are the traditions at stake.

The Kansas City Federal Reserve's September 2025 Beige Book, a report on economic conditions, says business contacts reported suppliers reluctant to lower prices even when tariff rates fell. This kept some costs for materials and parts from falling. Sources: [11].

The charity report is from April 2025 and names food and clothing among nonprofit costs. The Toy Association figure covers all U.S. toy sales, not shoebox items. Sources: [15], [13].
SJRes88_TR_support_05.response: No specific response to this point is provided.

SJRes88_TR_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.

  • Because Tariffs make goods from other countries cost more, which helps U.S. makers compete: “by making foreign goods more expensive, tariffs make domestic products more competitive.” [25] American Giant is one maker that produces in the United States: NPR reports that it “sources and manufactures almost all its products in the U.S., from cotton to the final stitch.” [26]
  • Because A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.” [27]
  • Because Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27]
  • Because Marriage and the husband's role as provider are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” [28] Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [28]
  • Because That family pattern also carries a duty to pass on the faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [28].
  • So By removing a defense against job and pay losses caused by imports, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
SJRes88_TR_oppose_01.response:
Response A price advantage for U.S. products does not establish that these taxes protect the men's jobs and pay on which the family argument depends.

  • Because The bill says the April 2 emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] The comparison is keeping or ending its import taxes as of October 30, 2025.
  • Because The family study ties marriage losses to men's earnings compared with women's: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27] The study looks at rising Chinese import competition during 1990–2014, not the effects of these taxes.
  • Because A study of local employment under the 2018–2019 taxes reports that “import tariffs do not appear to increase employment in manufacturing” [29]. That study directly tests the step from import protection to factory jobs, which the marriage study does not test.
  • Because A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–2019 taxes found that “a positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs.” [30]
  • Because For the 2025 taxes, the president of the textile trade group warned in October: “Reciprocal tariffs on these items hurt domestic textile producers and drives offshoring, undermining U.S. manufacturing jobs” [31]. Offshoring means moving production to other countries. She was discussing taxes on certain imported materials and machinery not available in the United States.
  • So American Giant's U.S. production and a price advantage do not establish that this extra tax layer preserves men's jobs or pay. Without that link, the historical import losses do not establish that ending these taxes puts marriage, husbands' provider roles or passing on the faith at greater risk.

The researchers Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. The researchers Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases lost jobs compared with less exposed industries. A positive protection effect was offset by input costs (the cost of materials and parts) and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [29], [30].

SJRes88_TR_oppose_02.support:
Point 2 Removing price protection for U.S. factory work also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.

  • Because A study using U.S. church data for 1990–2010 found that import shocks from China “led to a reduction in the number of churches” [32]. The study also found the shocks “caused an increase in the number of religious adherents” [32]. Adherents are members.
  • Because Members' money supports church life. The Southern Baptist faith statement calls for regular giving: “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally” [28]. Losing income leaves less money for that duty.
  • Because Losing local work can pull younger generations away from their congregations. The account of the closing of the Ragsdale Church of Christ reports, “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33].
  • Because A congregation is a place where families keep particular customs alive. Ragsdale's final gathering was “an old-time singing — the kind they used to have every fourth Sunday.” [33]
  • Because Worship there was also a family practice across generations. Member Emily Smartt “remembers being there with her parents and late husband.” [33]
  • So Ending this price protection for U.S. makers puts the jobs and income that help keep local congregations going at risk. Keeping those congregations and their shared customs alive honors [NAME]'s religious heritage. This gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.
SJRes88_TR_oppose_02.response:
Response The church evidence does not show that keeping these taxes protects local congregations or their inherited customs.

  • Because The cited church-study summary examines “trade shocks to manufacturing industries stemming from Chinese imports” [32], using U.S. church data for 1990–2010. Applying its finding to this bill requires a step it does not test: that ending this tax layer harms the jobs or income that support congregations.
  • Because Ragsdale's preacher reported that “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33]. That example shows one reason members leave. It supplies no link between those departures and the import taxes this bill ends.
  • So Neither source establishes that ending these taxes would cut church income or drive members away. The duty to give and the value of shared worship customs do not fill that gap. This Point has not shown that the bill threatens the congregations that carry those customs.

Ragsdale's preacher attributes the congregation's decline to location, societal changes and economics, including generational change. The summary of the study by Cesur and co-authors finds fewer churches and more adherents following Chinese import shocks in 1990-2010. Sources: [33], [32].

SJRES88_C01.support: The bill says “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [SES 1]

SJRES88_C02.support: Federal law says that when an emergency ends, “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [SES 2]. The Center for American Progress, a policy group that favors ending these taxes, says that ending this emergency “would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [UNN 3]

SJRES88_C03.support: An emergency ends if “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” [SES 2]. The bill says it acts “pursuant to section 202 of the National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1622)” [SES 1].

SJRES88_C04.support: The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [SES 23] It also says: “Should U.S. manufacturing capacity and output continue to worsen, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase duties under this order.” [UNC 10]

SJRES88_C05.support: A supply chain expert quoted by the magazine IndustryWeek said: “Most of these costs are likely to be passed along to American consumers.” [SEP 17] An October study of clothing imports said “U.S. importers, retailers, and consumers will shoulder much of the additional cost.” [UNC 4]

SJRES88_C06.support: Utilities buy pipes, pumps, valves, membranes and chemical treatments from around the world. The analysis says: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities.” [SEP 23] It adds that “water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” [SEP 23]

SJRES88_C07.support: Device makers refer to revenue “collected from reciprocal tariffs on medtech since April 2025” [SEP 3]. The American Hospital Association says tariffs “may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” [SEP 5] It also says that disruption “would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” [SEP 5].

SJRES88_C08.support: In Malaysia's deal the United States will “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [UNC 26] and identify goods “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [UNC 26] The September order says relief depends on factors including “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [UNN 29]. Malaysia's enforcement article says: “If a Party considers that the other Party has not complied with a provision of this Agreement, the Party may review the terms of this Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [UNN 35] Cambodia's agreement has a similar article [UNN 36].

SJRES88_C09.support:
The April 2 order lists among the practices it addresses “failures by governments in protecting labor and environment standards” [UNC 10] and “weak labor, environmental, and other regulatory standards and protections” [UNC 10]. It allows lower rates if a partner takes “significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters” [UNC 10]. The September order says earlier rate suspensions were “to reflect the fact that some trading partners had signaled a willingness to undertake meaningful economic and national security commitments with the United States” [SES 32].

The Malaysia statement lists promises in the same deal as the tariff terms: “Malaysia has committed to adopt and maintain high levels of environmental protection and to effectively enforce its environmental laws” [UNC 26] and “Malaysia has committed to refrain from banning, or imposing quotas on, exports to the United States of critical minerals or rare earth elements.” [UNC 26] The enforcement article applies if a country “has not complied with a provision of this Agreement” [UNN 35]. The Trade Representative said that if partners do not honor their agreements, “the president has his tariff authority,” [UNT 13] and that countries that do not comply “can have the tariffs go back into place.” [UNT 13] CNBC said it is not difficult to imagine that a country that agreed to buy goods “in order to avoid higher U.S. tariff rates might go back on that pledge” [UNT 13] if the court ruled against the tariffs.

SJRES88_C10.support: BBC reports: “President Trump’s threat to halt tariff talks has forced Thailand’s hand. It needs a deal to reduce the 36% tariff rate it is now facing.” [UNT 30] Reuters reports he urged the leaders “to end hostilities or risk their respective trade talks with Washington being put on hold.” [UNC 46] At the October signing he said: “We have to use that business to make sure they—they don't get into wars.” [UNC 48]

SJRES88_C11.support: Ending the emergency removes this order's power to change rates. An October analysis says other laws “have more limits and/or procedural steps than IEEPA” [UNC 14], the emergency powers law. The Congressional Research Service says IEEPA, unlike other tariff laws, “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [UNC 24] Treasury Secretary Bessent called the other authorities “not as efficient, not as powerful” [SES 12].
SJRES88_C11.response: Officials said the policy would continue another way. Trade adviser Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [UNC 13] Commerce Secretary Lutnick said: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [SES 11] An October 2025 analysis says other laws “could result in similar ends” [UNC 14]. So firms and markets could still face uncertainty about rates under other laws.

SJRES88_C12.support: China tied its charge to the U.S. tax: “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [UNN 24]. China later “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” [UNN 25]. In February 2026, after U.S. Customs stopped collecting these taxes, China said it would decide “whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original U.S. fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs.” [UNN 28]
SJRES88_C12.response: The cut came “following a U.S.-China economic and trade negotiation in Geneva” [UNN 25]. A repeal by Congress would be one-sided, not a negotiated exchange. A repeal does not change Chinese law. Other charges would remain: “certain U.S. agricultural products are also subject to Section 301 retaliatory tariffs” [UNN 25].

ui_copy.strengthGuide: Compare the overall case for each direction. Look at the different consequences in the accepted arguments. Consider all of the effects, not only the strongest one. Do not count headings. If two arguments describe the same consequence, count it once. Good evidence for an effect does not mean that the effect is large. There is no formula to calculate a winner. Choose Pending if you have no justified comparison.
ui_copy.mappingGuide: Does a shared claim seem too broad for this argument? Does a supporting path seem to be missing? Explain the problem in the optional note. Change your shared-claim answer only if your view of that claim changed. A coordinator reviews these notes. Your earlier answers stay saved.

ui_copy.coordinatorGuide: Review each mapping note and record one outcome: No mapping change, Mapping revised or Unresolved. A corrected mapping recomputes the outcomes.
